Two weeks ago, following a conversation with Jason Arday, Professor Simon Baron-Cohen posted a message on X.
The psychologist said he was “very concerned” about the impact of media coverage on his friend, who had autism, and linked it to work his Autism Research Centre at Cambridge University had done showing that autistic people were at a greater risk of suicide.
“This is relentless bullying of a vulnerable autistic man and raises safe-guarding issues,” he wrote. “It’s time to stop.” The site’s owner, Elon Musk, responded to the post with one word: “Liar”.
Yesterday, Baron-Cohen said Arday had sent him a voice note via WhatsApp on the morning of his death. “He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn’t coping with… he felt he couldn’t go on,” he told Radio 4’s Today programme.
In 2022, Baron-Cohen and psychologists from other UK universities found that autistic people had an elevated risk of suicide. They examined 372 coroners’ inquest reports over a three-year period to find out whether the person who died had been diagnosed with autism or had autistic traits. They found evidence of autism in more than 10% of those who died, compared with about 1.1% of the population overall.
Jill Aylott, founder of the National Autism and ADHD Assessment Centre, said: “accountability should never require us to abandon humanity.
“When somebody becomes the focus of sustained national criticism, particularly where that person is known to be neurodivergent, institutions should be asking: who is checking that this person is safe?”
Baron-Cohen said that for the last 10 days he had seen Arday’s mental health “getting worse and worse”.

article_body:
Jason Arday was found dead at his home in south London on Friday. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Jason Arday was found dead at his home in south London on Friday. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian Jason Arday This article is more than 1 month old Tributes paid to Jason Arday after former Cambridge professor’s death This article is more than 1 month old Andy Burnham calls for reflection after ‘tragedy on so many levels’ in comments echoed by London mayor Sadiq Khan
Prefer the Guardian on Google Andy Burnham has called the death of Jason Arday , whose body was found at his home in south London on Friday, a “tragedy on so many levels”.
Arday resigned as a professor at the University of Cambridge last week after allegations of plagiarism, which he denied. He was pronounced dead just after 3pm on Friday .
In a statement issued via his publisher, Simon & Schuster UK, the former academic’s family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.
Speaking to broadcasters during a visit to Cornwall on Saturday, the prime minister said: “It’s a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends. We think of them today.
“It’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how things came to this. A really sad, sad and sorry state of affairs and I think we all today think of Jason, his contribution and his family and friends.”
More than £20,000 has been raised for the family of Arday after the Windrush campaigner Sir Patrick Vernon launched a fundraising drive via GoFundMe in his memory.
Other leading figures to pay tribute included the London mayor, Sadiq Khan, and the Labour MP Bell Ribeiro-Addy.
Khan said: “I’m devastated for the family and friends of Jason Arday. He faced an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse. I know many Londoners will be angry and upset this evening.
“Jason Arday was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced. His death was a tragedy, but once again it should be a wake-up call for all of us.”
Speaking on Newsnight, Ribeiro-Addy read out a list of names including William O’Reilly, Ros Holmes, David Latchman, and Nicola Morrison. “These are all people that have actually proven to have been plagiarists, or people that have manipulated their data, and people that have been proven to have lifted whole pages from students’ papers or published work that they had to withdraw,” she said.
Ribeiro-Addy said there had been a media witch-hunt which was cruel because “it didn’t aim to just target him”.
“It aimed to target anybody that supported him, trying to isolate him as much as possible, going after people who had signed up to statements,” she said. “The difference between them and him was they were white, and he was not.”
The Conservative MP James Cleverly expressed his anger over Arday’s death. In a statement on X, he wrote that a number of people at academic institutions “have serious questions to answer”.
“They put him into positions he was clearly not qualified for so they could have a black wunderkind to show off, they pushed him into the spotlight for their own benefit,” they said. “His exposure was inevitable, a case of when, not if. His whole world fell apart.”
Simon Baron-Cohen, a clinical psychologist and the director of the Autism Research Centre, who was a friend of Arday’s, told Radio 4’s Today programme that he contacted him Friday morning and said that he felt he was unable to go on.
“He used those words in voice notes,” Baron-Cohen said. “At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.
“He was a vulnerable child, a vulnerable teenager and a vulnerable adult, so he needed and deserved safeguarding and support and reasonable adjustment every step of the way.”
Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to First Edition
Our morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it matters
Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another person’s work in his PhD thesis, but denied all allegations. A review conducted by Liverpool John Moores University, where he completed his doctorate, upheld its decision to award him a PhD earlier this year.
In recent weeks, other elements of his life story were increasingly questioned , including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running. He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal as a child.
The National Education Union general secretary, Daniel Kebede, said Arday had been subjected to “a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism”.
“I don’t believe this was ever simply about ‘professional conduct’ or ‘plagiarism’,” he said.
“There is a profound difference between scrutiny and a sustained public campaign that turns an individual into a symbol of everything the right believes is wrong with DEI.
“The effect has been chilling. It tells Black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target.
“A target not only for criticism of your work, but for a much broader political and cultural backlash.”
The Metropolitan police said his death was being treated as unexpected, but not believed to be suspicious.

article_body:
We use cookies where necessary to allow us to understand how people interact with our website and content, so that we can continue to improve our service.
Dr Arday’s death was the direct result of media harassment – we’re demanding a public inquiry to prevent this from ever happening again
Before his death on Friday, Dr Jason Arday was subject to a barrage of racist, ableist and cruel media attention, which continued to escalate even after his resignation on August 5th.
The press attention was unrelenting. 249 articles were published in 22 days, mostly led by the broadsheets. This wasn’t a tabloid scandal – the journalists involved were often public figures in their own right.
A resignation normally causes the media to back off, but they only produced more content. Stories about Jason were driving clicks – with outlets like The Times even putting out paid adverts for their articles .
In his resignation letter, Dr Jason Arday said to his supporters “you have carried me through some of the darkest moments of my life”; “I need time to heal”; “space to begin again” and that he had “reached the limits of what any person should reasonably be expected to endure.”
Jason wasn’t the only one asking the press to stop.
Professor Simon Baron Cohen released a statement on July 31st, leaning on his expertise in autism, stating:
“I’m very concerned about the impact of the media coverage on Professor Jason Arday who is autistic.
He has been accused of plagiarism and he was cleared of any academic misconduct following a rigorous investigation by Liverpool John Moores University.
And yet he continues to be systematically discredited over every detail of his life, daily. We should of course always investigate plagiarism to protect academic standards.
However, I cannot stand by and watch when an autistic man is on the ground and the kicking continues. This is relentless bullying of a vulnerable autistic man and raises safe-guarding issues. It’s time to stop.”
The day afterwards, the Guardian published an article titled “Playbooks, plagiarism and a pig’s head: new claims surrounding a star Cambridge professor”.
Before this article was published, details of it were sent to Jason to give him an opportunity to respond. His supporters contacted The Guardian about this piece. A letter was sent to Katharine Viner, the Editor-in-Chief of the Guardian, and separate contact was made with the journalist writing the piece.
This article dissected Jason’s claims about his personal life, and the Guardian featured it on their podcast, Today In Focus. A reel the Guardian posted of that podcast, where the claims within the article were played for laughs, has since been deleted.
The Guardian’s coverage continued after Arday’s resignation, interviewing people who knew Jason as a child to question whether he was really non-verbal. The intense focus on Jason’s background and disability was widespread, with The Daily Mail even carrying a piece from a psychiatrist pondering a diagnosis for Jason, tempered only by the context that “I should say that I’ve never met Jason Arday, and so have no idea what has been going on in his mind, or how much truth there may or may not be in his life story.”
During the escalating coverage, those who supported Arday received countless requests for interviews and quotes.
These journalists were often warned about Jason’s wellbeing, and were still not dissuaded from chasing the story.
The writer and broadcaster Nels Abbey and Lord Simon Woolley , the Principal of Homerton College, both expressed their concerns.
Nels shared an example of this type of correspondence from the 3rd of August with a journalist during the firestorm, explicitly making clear his concern for Jason’s wellbeing.
Despite warnings from those around Jason trying to safeguard him from the onslaught, the stories kept coming.
Hours after Jason died, The Times ran a (now deleted) story headlined “Jason Arday may want to get himself a nice pair of orange trousers”.
Whilst this continued, the racist and eugenist academic Nathan Cofnas, who instigated the story, gave a little remarked upon interview to a right-wing youtuber, joking: “ After the revolution, I’ll be the head of the dept of eugenics & race science at Harvard.”
We believe that the press must be held accountable for their racist, profit-motivated conduct that led to Jason’s death. We’re calling for a public inquiry into how to ensure a responsible press given its contribution to Dr Arday’s tragic death.

title_zh: 媒体忽视Jason Arday心理健康警告的影响
summary_zh: 本文讨论了媒体对自闭症人士Jason Arday的报道可能带来的负面影响。文章引用了对Arday心理健康的担忧，指出媒体在报道中未能充分考虑其自闭症（autism）背景，可能加剧了对其的误解和偏见。专家强调，媒体的关注应更加谨慎，以避免对Arday及其他自闭症人士造成伤害。整体而言，文章呼吁媒体在报道此类敏感话题时，需更加关注受影响者的心理健康和社会影响。
l1_lead: 媒体在报道自闭症人士Jason Arday时忽视其心理健康背景，可能加剧误解与偏见，呼吁更谨慎的报道以保护受影响者。
l2_summary:
本文探讨了媒体对自闭症人士Jason Arday的报道可能带来的负面影响，特别是对其心理健康的潜在威胁。文章指出，媒体在报道中未能充分考虑Arday的自闭症背景，导致对他的误解和偏见加剧。专家们强调，媒体在关注此类敏感话题时，应更加谨慎，以避免对Arday及其他自闭症人士造成进一步的伤害。报道中提到的心理健康担忧，反映了社会对自闭症人士的普遍误解，这种误解不仅影响了公众对他们的看法，也可能对他们的心理健康产生负面影响。

整体而言，文章呼吁媒体在报道涉及自闭症及相关心理健康问题时，需更加关注受影响者的心理健康和社会影响。通过对Arday案例的分析，作者希望引起媒体和公众对自闭症人士心理健康问题的重视，促使媒体在报道时采取更为负责任的态度，以减少对自闭症人士的偏见和误解。

body:

article_body:
Listen to this article with a free profile 00:00 00:00 Jason Arday in London in 2023. Ken McKay / ITV via Shutterstock Share Add NBC News to Google Aug. 14, 2026, 4:28 PM EDT / Updated Aug. 15, 2026, 10:45 AM EDT By Marlene Lenthang A former Cambridge professor was found dead at his London home on Friday, one week after he resigned from his position at the esteemed university following accusations of plagiarism.
Jason Arday, 41, became the youngest Black professor at Cambridge when he was hired as a professor of sociology of education in 2023.
London’s Metropolitan Police force said it responded to a report of a man found unresponsive inside a property on Friday and that the man was pronounced dead at the scene, without naming Arday. Authorities said the death is being treated as “unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.”
“We are desperately saddened to hear this tragic news. Our heartfelt sympathies go to Jason Arday’s family and friends at this incredibly difficult time,” University of Cambridge Vice-Chancellor Deborah Prentice said Friday.
Arday was known for his neurodivergence; he had said he was diagnosed with autism as a child and was unable to speak until the age of 11. He went on to forge a path in academia as a scholar of race, inequality and education.
Arday had resigned on Aug. 5 following scrutiny over alleged plagiarism in his academic work and questions about his accomplishments.
Last month, questions regarding his qualifications were raised publicly by Nathan Cofnas, a former Cambridge philosophy researcher who left the institution after critiquing diversity, equity and inclusion programs.
The Times of London had subsequently published an analysis of Arday’s 2015 Ph.D. thesis highlighting passages that it said were “identical or near-identical” to an earlier paper written by another researcher.
In the weeks since, British media outlets led intense and prolonged scrutiny of Arday’s work, also interrogating a history of claims about his childhood and personal life.
A statement from Arday’s family said he was “a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone,” condemning critics who they said “would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him.”
Cambridge professor Simon Baron-Cohen, director of the university’s Autism Research Centre, told the BBC he was in touch with Arday hours before his death.
He said Arday “was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life,” adding that he “wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn’t go on.”
Baron-Cohen said that Arday had believed “there was a racist playbook to discredit Black academics in universities, and that they used accusations of plagiarism to try and bring down Black academics,” adding that Arday referred to former Harvard President Claudine Gay , who resigned two years ago while facing plagiarism allegations and criticism over her comments on antisemitism.
British Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Saturday that the death was “a tragedy on so many levels,” adding that “it’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say.”

London Mayor Sadiq Khan said on X that Arday had faced “an unacceptable public hounding and campaign of abuse” and that he “was the victim of a pernicious public shaming that other people in his position simply wouldn’t have faced.”
Hacked Off, a campaign group that supports regulation of the media, called for an “inquiry into the culture and behaviour of the British press” following the death, saying scrutiny “went far beyond any limited public interest considerations around academic standards.”
While Cambridge initially defended Arday, on Aug. 5 it opened an investigation “following new information about Professor Arday’s qualifications and honorary appointments.”
In his resignation statement last week, Arday described his tenure as “the privilege of my life to teach my students,” but conceded “the years since my appointment have also been marked by an unrelenting level of public scrutiny and personal attack.”
“While criticism is an inevitable part of academic life, what I have experienced has gone far beyond scholarly disagreement. The relentless accusations, speculation and public commentary have taken a profound toll on me and on those I love,” he continued.
In a statement Thursday, Cambridge’s Prentice shared an update on the inquiry into Arday, saying the university would investigate the circumstances around his appointment by the Faculty of Education in 2022 and his time at Cambridge.
She also said she asked the university council’s deputy chair and council’s audit committee to establish terms for an independent review of all university processes that will take place alongside the probe into Arday.
In his resignation announcement, Arday said he reached a point where the “personal cost becomes too great.”
“For my own wellbeing, for my family, and for those who have stood by me throughout this difficult period, I have concluded that the only way to bring this chapter to an end is to step away,” he said.
Arday’s memoir, “Great and Unfortunate Things,” was released earlier this week in the U.S., giving an account of his childhood — from being diagnosed with autism and developmental delays at the age of 3 — to speaking by the age of 11 and reading and writing by the age of 18.
“Without romanticizing the struggle, this is a story of determination against seemingly insurmountable odds — and of a family and a small group of believers whose compassion helped him see what is possible,” a description for the book by publisher Simon & Schuster said.

title_zh: 剑桥前教授贾森·阿尔代因抄袭指控辞职一周后被发现死亡
summary_zh: 贾森·阿尔代（Jason Arday）是一位曾任剑桥大学教授的学者，因抄袭指控而辞职。文章指出，他在辞职前遭受了无情的审视和嘲笑，感到无法承受职业和声誉的双重损失。阿尔代认为，存在一个种族主义的剧本，旨在通过抄袭指控来打击黑人学者。他的观点强调了在学术界中，针对黑人学者的抹黑行为及其对个人心理健康的严重影响。
l1_lead: 贾森·阿尔代因抄袭指控辞职后自杀，揭示了学术界对黑人学者的抹黑及其对心理健康的深远影响。
l2_summary: 贾森·阿尔代（Jason Aldine）是一位曾任剑桥大学教授的学者，近期因抄袭指控辞职，随后被发现死亡。阿尔代在辞职前经历了严厉的审视和公众的嘲笑，这使他感到难以承受职业和声誉的双重打击。他在接受采访时提到，自己认为这一切背后存在一个种族主义的剧本，旨在通过抄袭指控来打击黑人学者。他的观点揭示了在学术界中，针对黑人学者的抹黑行为不仅影响了他们的职业生涯，也对其心理健康造成了严重的负面影响。阿尔代的遭遇引发了对学术界中种族歧视问题的广泛关注，尤其是在当前社会对种族平等和公正的讨论日益增多的背景下。此事件不仅反映了个体在面对不公正指控时的脆弱，也突显了学术界在处理种族问题时的复杂性和挑战。阿尔代的死让人深思，如何在学术环境中建立一个更加包容和公正的氛围，以保护所有学者的声誉和心理健康。

title: Surely Liberals Can Agree That Plagiarism Is Bad - persuasion.community
body:
原话：“1 in 4 autistic people have planned or attempted suicide. That’s why I’m very concerned about the impact of the media coverage on Professor Jason Arday who is autistic.”
论点：他对自闭症人士的关注是因为1/4的自闭症患者曾计划或尝试自杀。

quotes: 1 in 4 autistic people have planned or attempted suicide. That’s why I’m very concerned about the impact of the media coverage on Professor Jason Arday who is autistic.
topic_zh: 对自闭症人士媒体报道影响的关注
claim_zh: 他对自闭症人士的关注是因为1/4的自闭症患者曾计划或尝试自杀。
article_body:
Sam Kahn Aug 03, 2026 373 15 58 Share Cambridge University’s Senate House. (Photo by Joe Giddens/PA Images via Getty Images.) This is a nasty story.
In 2023, Jason Arday made international news for becoming, at age 37, the youngest black professor in the history of Cambridge University. It wasn’t just that, though. Arday had a really remarkable background. Raised on a council estate in south London, Arday was, in his account, diagnosed at age three with autism and global development delay and didn’t speak until he was 11. At that point, something “clicked,” as he has put it, but he wouldn’t read or write until he was 18.
Then, Arday really applied himself. By age 30, he obtained a Ph.D. in Educational Studies from Liverpool John Moores University, and, according to his official biography , worked at Roehampton, Durham, and Glasgow before being appointed to a highly prestigious professorship at Cambridge. In his spare time, Arday was an ultra long-distance runner, in 2010 completing 30 marathons in 35 days and over two decades raising £5.5 million for charity.
It’s a beautiful story—Arday himself for the documentary “Great Big Story” said of his life, “Wouldn’t it be the most ridiculous story ever told?”—and it’s about to be commemorated in a memoir that Simon & Schuster UK is releasing later this month.
The only problem is that large portions of it may not be true.
In 2023, only months after his appointment at Cambridge, a pair of academics, Dave Harris and Martyn Hammersley, raised concerns to Cambridge, to Liverpool John Moores, and to different journals Arday had published in about the academic integrity of Arday’s work. Two of the journals issued corrections . Cambridge replied that the issues preceded Arday’s hiring and therefore were not within Cambridge’s “remit” to investigate. Liverpool John Moores, for its part, has issued a statement that the university in 2025 conducted a “confidential procedure” in response to the allegations and that “Professor Arday’s PhD still stands.”
Persuasion is a registered nonprofit that relies on reader support to pay our staff and keep our content free for everyone. If you value our work and want to fight for liberal values wherever they are threatened, please become a paying subscriber today!
In 2025, the Times Higher Education spiked an article about the allegations against Arday after Arday enlisted the defamation law firm Carter-Ruck to send a letter to the publication. But last month, Nathan Cofnas, a former Fellow at Cambridge, published a post on Substack that blew the Arday story wide open. Using the plagiarism detector Copyleaks, Cofnas found over 30 cases of “substantial overlap” in Arday’s Ph.D. dissertation with the previously-published dissertation of Paula Zwozdiak-Myers , many of them long chunks of verbatim copying, as well as verbatim copying from other sources. Cofnas went through ten other papers of Arday’s, taken from Arday’s own list of “principal and recent publications,” and found significant issues, including plagiarism, in at least four of them. Additional malfeasance included virtually identical quotes attributed to different sources in different papers, which strongly implies that at least some of the quotes from supposed participants in his studies were confabulated .
Meanwhile, Cofnas raised difficult questions about aspects of Arday’s personal story. He noted that running 30 marathons in 35 days would place Arday in the ultra-marathon elite—this without having left any ostensible mark in the running community. “If Arday [did that], I’ll eat my yarmulke,” said Cofnas by telephone. The claim to have raised £5.5 million for charity has already been walked back by Arday, who in a recent interview said the fundraising was done in conjunction with collectives. And Cofnas found that Arday’s two GCSE qualifications—in physical education and textiles—were unobtainable without passing written tests, a detail that challenges the timeline given by Arday that he could not read or write until he was 18. Cofnas also suggests that Arday’s account of his speech development is “medically improbable.”
Cofnas is far from a neutral party in this case. He was fired by Cambridge’s Emmanuel College in 2024 on the back of student protests against him for a Substack post in which he wrote that in a color-blind meritocracy “blacks would disappear from almost all high-profile positions outside of sports and entertainment.” Harris, the academic who first raised questions about Arday’s scholarship, was embroiled in a controversy of his own in which he had his emeritus title at Plymouth Marjon University stripped for a time after he critiqued critical race theory.
How To Fix DEI Rachel Kleinfeld · September 26, 2024 Read full story The fact that his accusers are controversial in their own right may help to explain why so many academics have reflexively defended Arday. In an interview with The Times of London, Arday this week said , “There has been, since I arrived at Cambridge, a very well orchestrated and co-ordinated campaign to unseat me from my position. The motive is racially motivated. I think there’s a reason why it’s me, and I do think that reason is aligned to ableism and racism.” In 2025, when the allegations against Arday were beginning to surface, the Cambridge professors Simon Baron-Cohen and Ricardo Sabates circulated an open letter under the heading “URGENT PLEASE SIGN ANTI-RACISM LETTER FOR JASON ARDAY.” The Good Law Project, an activist organization, orchestrated a solidarity letter last week that has been signed by 14,000 people decrying the “sustained and malicious attacks on the academic integrity of Dr. Jason Arday,” which the letter attributed to “an attempt to undermine Black people who hold positions of influence.” And Cambridge University has wholeheartedly taken Arday’s side. A university spokesperson said , “Professor Arday has been the victim of a vile campaign to undermine his credibility, which must stop.”
So—as you can see—it’s an uncomfortable story landing right on the faultlines of the culture wars. On one side is institutional procedure alongside an institutional culture hyper-sensitive to accusations against what the Good Law Project calls “a working class Black man.” On the other side is the argument that standards must be maintained—and maintained by academic and journalistic vigilantes if the institutions are unwilling to uphold their own meritocratic principles.
And of course the real issue isn’t exactly Arday. It’s the presumption that the politically progressive culture ascendant at Cambridge and in higher education in general has long ago deviated from real meritocracy. By phone, Cofnas was clear on that point. He said, “This is a story about DEI and the corruption that is required to sustain the system of DEI—of elevating people based on identity characteristics rather than merit.”
So what do we do in a case like this, where everybody pretty much sees what they are already predisposed to see? Well, first of all, we look at the source material—and in this case it’s pretty unequivocal. For instance, Arday’s line on page 17 of his 2015 dissertation—“Student teachers are unique individuals and differ in their personal biographies and prior experiences, disposition to enquiry, cognitive and perceptive abilities, communication, interpersonal skills, adaptability, values, and belief systems”—is a perfect match to page 1 of Zwozdiak-Myers’ 2009 dissertation . According to Cofnas, the pattern is repeated dozens of times, while The Telegraph for its part found “more than 100 passages that are identical or nearly identical” to Zwozdiak-Myers’ thesis. There is, as Harris put it , “no other plausible explanation” than plagiarism for the overlaps.
Then, in the week following Cofnas’ Substack post, subsequent reporting found additional patterns of fabulism by Arday. In an open letter to a government minister last year, Arday said he was the victim of innumerable threats and attacks since he took up his Cambridge position. In an interview with The Guardian this week, Arday clarified that he was referring to, among other incidents, a “severed pig’s head” that had been sent to his parents’ London home. That assertion triggered a macabre scavenger hunt, with Guardian journalists visiting the butcher shop that Arday claimed had sold the pig to the assailant. But the butcher said that there had been no police investigation into the incident, as Arday had asserted. For their part, London’s Metropolitan Police said that the details Arday gave of a police investigation into the incident were “categorically” inaccurate.
Arday further claimed that a masked man had accosted him twice at his Cambridge faculty building and threatened him with a knife the second time. But as The Guardian noted, no intruder appeared on CCTV on either occasion, and Arday did not inform colleagues or interrupt his working day after the alleged knife incident.
Meanwhile, a recently-surfaced video interview with Arday appears to show him claiming that he starred in the acclaimed documentary “Seven Up”—a mathematical impossibility unless Arday was actually born in 1956. And just today Glasgow University has denied Arday’s claim that he held a visiting professorship there.
Given all that—the all-but-indisputable evidence of plagiarism, in addition to the patterns of fanciful statements by Arday—the case for his defense collapses. “I think it’s plagiarism and it’s obvious,” one academic told The Guardian under condition of anonymity. “There is no question that there is extensive plagiarism,” David Sanders, an independent researcher who reviewed Arday’s case last year for Times Higher Education , said to Retraction Watch.
What Being a Digital Nomad Taught Me About the Real World Sam Kahn · Jul 27 Read full story Arday, for his part, did not, in a wide-ranging interview he gave to The Times of London last week, directly challenge the primary allegation of plagiarism and academic misconduct. He said, “I am accountable for the mistakes I’ve made. I hold myself accountable and other people should hold me accountable.” Instead, he took another line of defense, contending, “We’re talking about academia here. I didn’t murder somebody. I think the cruelty that I’ve experienced and the positioning of me as this kind of liar and fantasist is totally unacceptable.”
If it’s fair to say that the preponderance of evidence at this point speaks to serious academic misconduct on Arday’s part, the next question—picking up on Arday’s lead—is to ask ourselves what the stakes are here and what the story is really about. Arday is right of course that one academic with a shaky relationship to the truth is not, by itself, a huge deal. But, unfortunately for Arday’s defense, it is a story with more reach than he admits and it really does indict the institutions backing him.
For one thing, there is the issue of how Arday and his supporters have tried to defend him. There has been very little of the accountability Arday has called for—and there has been no willingness to look at the very obvious evidence of academic misconduct. The overriding tendency has been to shoot the messenger and to go after the academics, particularly Harris and Cofnas, who called attention to the issues in Arday’s work. According to The Guardian, Arday attempted to lodge a police complaint against Harris. article_body:
David Hughes | Izzie Addison | Michael Howie , Senior News Editor 15 August 2026 News Briefings

Andy Burnham has called the death of former Cambridge professor Jason Arday a “tragedy” that should be a “moment for reflection”.
Prof Arday, who resigned after a plagiarism row, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called an address in Battersea, south London, on Friday to reports that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property.
He told a friend he “couldn’t go on” hours before he died after being subjected to intense scrutiny over his academic career.
The Prime Minister told reporters during a visit to Cornwall: “It’s a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends. We think of think of them today.
“It’s not a moment for any rushing to judgment. It’s a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how how things came to this.
“A really sad, sad and sorry state of affairs and I think we all today think of Jason, his contribution, and his family and friends.”
Jason Arday was found dead on Friday ES Prof Arday said he felt he “couldn’t go on” hours before he died, a friend revealed earlier on Saturday.
Prof Arday was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to Daley Thompson Way, in Battersea , just after 3pm on Friday to reports that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property.
The Metropolitan Police said his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.
Prof Arday last week resigned as professor of sociology of education at Cambridge .
A series of media reports alleged he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.
Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million for charity.
Ex-Cambridge professor Jason Arday found dead at south London address
London bus drivers 'passing out' due to extreme heat

Winter escapes and activities to end the year in style
An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Prof Arday of wrongdoing.
University of Cambridge professor, and director of the Autism Research Centre, Sir Simon Baron-Cohen told the BBC he spoke to Prof Arday on Friday morning.
Jason Arday was a professor of sociology of education at Cambridge University AFP/Getty Sir Simon told Radio 4’s Today programme: “He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn’t go on.”
“He used those words in voice notes,” he added.
Sir Simon said: “At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.
“He was a vulnerable child, a vulnerable teenager, and a vulnerable adult, so he needed and deserved safeguarding and support and reasonable adjustment every step of the way.”
Sir Simon said Prof Arday was a “kind and gentle” man who had been “bombarded by every media outlet” and used as a “lightning rod” to examine diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.
Sir Simon told the BBC that plagiarism allegations made by another academic, Nathan Cofnas – who has reportedly defined himself as a “race realist” – opened up a “media frenzy”.
He said: “Jason was being used as almost like a lightning rod to examine this policy of DEI, and Jason was bombarded by every media outlet to paint him as a fraud.”
The cognitive neuroscientist said he had grown concerned about the mental health of Prof Arday, a “vulnerable autistic man” that he could see was struggling.
Andy Burnham spoke about Jason Arday’s tragic death on a visit to Cornwall on Saturday PA Sir Simon said: “In the last 10 days, I’ve witnessed his mental health getting worse and worse, as the media didn’t stop ridiculing him, humiliating him, discrediting him.
“As I said, yesterday morning, his last voice note was that he just couldn’t go on.
“We need to let the investigations proceed, we need to understand how this tragedy has happened, but there has to be accountability at lots of levels.”
In a statement on Saturday, National Education Union (NEU) general secretary Daniel Kebede said Prof Arday had been subjected to “a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism”.
He added: “I don’t believe this was ever simply about ‘professional conduct’ or ‘plagiarism’.
“There is a profound difference between scrutiny and a sustained public campaign that turns an individual into a symbol of everything the right believes is wrong with DEI.
“The effect has been chilling. It tells black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target.
“A target not only for criticism of your work, but for a much broader political and cultural backlash.”

article_body:
Jason Arday quit his role as professor of sociology of education this month. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian View image in fullscreen Jason Arday quit his role as professor of sociology of education this month. Photograph: Christian Sinibaldi/The Guardian Jason Arday This article is more than 1 month old Cambridge University defends its mental health support for Jason Arday This article is more than 1 month old University says it continued to provide support after resignation of academic, who was found dead on Friday
Prefer the Guardian on Google The University of Cambridge has defended its mental health support for the academic Jason Arday.
The university said it had continued to provide Arday with extensive mental health support and security measures, including installing panic alarms and screening racist emails and post, after he resigned from his post as professor of sociology of education this month.
He quit after widespread press coverage of accusations of plagiarism and inconsistencies in statements about his career and achievements .
A University of Cambridge spokesperson said: “Our support continued in the face of intense public and media scrutiny and after his resignation. Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with Jason’s family and loved ones at this extremely difficult time.”
Arday, 41, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to his home in Battersea, south London, on Friday.
When he was appointed professor of sociology of education at Cambridge at the age of 37 in 2023, he was the university’s youngest ever black professor.
A vigil in Arday’s memory organised by the campaign group Stand Up to Racism will be held on the steps of the National Gallery in Trafalgar Square, central London, at 6pm on Monday. The group’s co-convener Weyman Bennett said in a statement that Arday’s death was the “result of a racist witch-hunt”.
He added: “For more than a week, the rightwing press, politicians and the far right have hounded Jason with the most vicious racism. They are spreading the far-right lie that black people are only appointed because of the colour of our skin, rather than our ability.”
View image in fullscreen Prof Deborah Prentice, the vice-chancellor of Cambridge University, said her top priority was ‘supporting our community through this tragedy’. Photograph: Linda Nylind/The Guardian Arday was initially accused of plagiarising another academic’s work for his PhD thesis. He denied the accusations, and an investigation by Liverpool John Moores University this year upheld its decision to award him a PhD.
When allegations surfaced in the UK media in July, Cambridge said it had investigated the claims and found no wrongdoing, describing Arday as the victim of a “vile smear campaign to undermine his credibility”.
This month, the university announced it would open a fresh investigation after it said it received “new information” about Arday’s qualifications and career.
Other elements of Arday’s life story were increasingly questioned, including claims of prodigious money-raising for charity and feats of long-distance running. He was also challenged about whether he was nonverbal until the age of 11, as well as being illiterate until 18.
It is understood Cambridge has paused the investigation while Arday’s family are grieving, and will consider whether to reopen it in due course.
Academics and politicians have cast doubt on whether Cambridge took Arday’s vulnerability seriously when he was appointed to the ­senior public-facing role in 2023. At the time, the university had been facing criticism for its lack of diversity in senior roles.
Prof Simon Baron-Cohen, Arday’s friend and former colleague, told Times Radio he thought the university should proceed with the investigation. “We should see what we learn from it. This is the whole purpose of investigations,” he said.
He also questioned whether the media had failed in its duty of care towards Arday, as a vulnerable person with disabilities. He said Arday faced racist abuse and was used as a “lightning rod for a culture war on [diversity, equity and inclusion]”.
Simon Woolley, the principal of Homerton College, Cambridge, and Arday’s former mentor, has called for an investigation into the “vicious media onslaught”.
In a statement on Saturday, Prof Deborah Prentice, the vice-chancellor of Cambridge University, said her “thoughts and deepest condolences” were with Arday’s family, as well as with colleagues and students in the faculty of education and at Jesus College where he was a fellow.
“Supporting our community through this tragedy is the single most important priority for me and my leadership team right now. We will be reaching out to many of you directly, and we are committed to ensuring that no one feels they must face this alone,” she said.
A fundraiser launched by the Windrush campaigner Patrick Vernon on Saturday afternoon has raised more than £65,000 to contribute towards funeral and memorial costs and support for Arday’s family.
On the crowdfunder’s webpage, Vernon said: “I was one of the people who publicly supported Jason during the recent controversy because I was deeply concerned about the nature and intensity of the attacks directed towards him. I was also subject to media scrutiny for signing the letter of support and challenged in supporting Jason.”
Andy Burnham, the prime minister, described Arday’s death as a “tragedy on so many levels” and urged a “moment of reflection”.
In a statement issued via Simon & Schuster, which published Arday’s memoir, Great and Unfortunate Things, in the US this week, Arday’s family said they were “in shock to have lost this amazing father, partner, brother, uncle and son”.
They added: “Jason was subjected to a campaign of sustained abuse for more than three years since he accepted the role of professor at Cambridge University by those who would leave no stone unturned in their quest to undermine him. The campaign of misinformation was too much for Jason, who was a gentle man and who always wanted to see the best in everyone.”
title_zh: 剑桥大学为杰森·阿尔代的心理健康支持辩护
summary_zh: 本文讨论了剑桥大学对杰森·阿尔代（Jason Arday）心理健康支持的辩护。阿尔代面临种族歧视的攻击，并被视为“多样性、公平和包容”（diversity, equity and inclusion）文化战争的“导火索”。文章强调，大学应继续调查以获取更多信息，并质疑媒体对阿尔代照顾的责任。剑桥大学认为，调查的目的在于学习和理解事件的深层次原因。
l1_lead: 剑桥大学为杰森·阿尔代的心理健康支持辩护，强调需深入调查事件原因，并质疑媒体对其照顾的责任。
l2_summary:
剑桥大学近日为杰森·阿尔代（Jason Arday）提供的心理健康支持进行了辩护，强调了在面对种族歧视攻击和“多样性、公平和包容”（diversity, equity and inclusion）文化战争中，大学的责任和角色。阿尔代被视为这一文化争论的“导火索”，其经历引发了广泛的关注和讨论。文章指出，剑桥大学认为，继续对事件进行深入调查是必要的，目的是为了更好地理解事件的深层次原因，而不仅仅是表面现象。

在此背景下，大学质疑媒体在报道阿尔代心理健康照顾方面的责任，认为媒体的叙述可能未能全面反映事件的复杂性。剑桥大学的立场是，调查不仅是为了回应外界的压力，更是为了从中学习，以便在未来能够更有效地支持面临类似挑战的学生。通过这种方式，大学希望能够推动更广泛的对话，促进对心理健康问题的理解和重视。

总的来说，剑桥大学的辩护强调了在多元文化背景下，教育机构在保护学生心理健康方面的重要性，以及在面对社会争议时，如何通过深入调查和反思来提升自身的支持体系。这一立场不仅反映了对阿尔代个人经历的关注，也体现了对更广泛社会问题的思考，呼吁社会各界共同关注和解决心理健康问题。

title: Jason Arday, former Cambridge professor, told friend he ‘couldn’t go on’ hours before his death - The Journal
body:
原话：“He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn’t go on.” / “At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.” / “In the last 10 days, I’ve witnessed his mental health getting worse and worse, as the media didn’t stop ridiculing him, humiliating him, discrediting him.”
论点：媒体的持续攻击导致Jason Arday的心理健康恶化，最终使他感到无法继续生活。
论据：他在最后的语音信息中表示自己‘无法继续下去’。

At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.
In the last 10 days, I’ve witnessed his mental health getting worse and worse, as the media didn’t stop ridiculing him, humiliating him, discrediting him.
topic_zh: 媒体对个人的影响
claim_zh: 媒体的持续攻击导致Jason Arday的心理健康恶化，最终使他感到无法继续生活。

Close Best of the Box Irish News FactCheck Voices Investigates Gaeilge Sign In Sign out sections Voices FactCheck Investigates Gaeilge Quizzes Money Diaries Explainers The Journal TV topics Irish News Politics World News Elections --> Climate Crisis Housing Cost of Living Road Safety Courts Ukraine Gaza Newsletters FactCheck Temperature Check Inside the Newsroom The Journal Investigates See all newsletters --> Magazines Daft.ie Property Allianz Home The 42 Sport TG4 Entertainment Domino's Best of the Box Podcasts The Explainer A deep dive into one big news story The 42FM Sport meets news, current affairs, society & pop culture See all podcasts --> Sign in to have your say Or create a free account to join the discussion Advertisement More Stories Jason Arday Joe Giddens/PA RIP Jason Arday, former Cambridge professor, told friend he ‘couldn’t go on’ hours before his death National Education Union (NEU) general secretary Daniel Kebede said Arday had been subjected to “a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism”. 11.52am, 15 Aug 2026 21.1k Share options Copy link Email Facebook X FORMER UNIVERSITY OF Cambridge professor Jason Arday told a friend he felt he “couldn’t go on” hours before he died.
Arday, who resigned after a plagiarism row, was pronounced dead after emergency services were called to his home in Battersea, London, just after 3pm on Friday to reports that a man had been found unresponsive inside a property.
The Metropolitan Police said his death is being treated as unexpected, but is not believed to be suspicious.
University of Cambridge professor and director of the Autism Research Centre Simon Baron-Cohen told the BBC he spoke to Arday on Friday morning.
Baron-Cohen told Radio 4’s Today programme: “He was being subjected to relentless scrutiny, including ridicule, discrediting absolutely every detail of his life, and he wasn’t coping with the loss of his career, the loss of his reputation, and he felt he couldn’t go on.”
“He used those words in voice notes,” he added.
Baron-Cohen said: “At the heart of all of this was a man who’d been diagnosed in childhood with disabilities that included autism and language delay and learning differences.
“He was a vulnerable child, a vulnerable teenager, and a vulnerable adult, so he needed and deserved safeguarding and support and reasonable adjustment every step of the way.”
Baron-Cohen said Arday was a “kind and gentle” man who had been “bombarded by every media outlet” and used as a “lightning rod” to examine diversity, equity and inclusion (DEI) policies.
Arday, a professor of sociology of education who became Cambridge’s youngest black professor in 2023, quit following a series of media reports alleging he plagiarised his PhD thesis – completed at Liverpool John Moores University – and other research.
Further questions were asked in the press about the truth of other claims he made, including saying he ran 600 miles in six days and that he had raised £5.5 million (€6.44 million) for charity.
An investigation at Liverpool John Moores University cleared Arday of wrongdoing.
Baron-Cohen told the BBC that plagiarism allegations made by another academic, Nathan Cofnas – who has reportedly defined himself as a “race realist” – opened up a “media frenzy”.
He said: “Jason was being used as almost like a lightning rod to examine this policy of DEI, and Jason was bombarded by every media outlet to paint him as a fraud.”
The cognitive neuroscientist said he had grown concerned about the mental health of Arday, a “vulnerable autistic man” that he could see was struggling.
Baron-Cohen said: “In the last 10 days, I’ve witnessed his mental health getting worse and worse, as the media didn’t stop ridiculing him, humiliating him, discrediting him.
“As I said, yesterday morning, his last voice note was that he just couldn’t go on.
“We need to let the investigations proceed, we need to understand how this tragedy has happened, but there has to be accountability at lots of levels.”
In a statement on Saturday, National Education Union (NEU) general secretary Daniel Kebede said Arday had been subjected to “a public and brutal takedown that unleashed a tirade of racism”.
He added: “I don’t believe this was ever simply about ‘professional conduct’ or ‘plagiarism’.
“There is a profound difference between scrutiny and a sustained public campaign that turns an individual into a symbol of everything the right believes is wrong with DEI.
“The effect has been chilling. It tells black people and others from underrepresented backgrounds that entering prominent public positions will make you a target.
“A target not only for criticism of your work, but for a much broader political and cultural backlash.”
Speaking to reporters while on a visit to southwest England, UK prime minister Andy Burnham said it was “not a moment for any rushing to judgement”.
“It’s a tragedy on so many levels, but particularly just for everybody who knew Jason, his family obviously, his friends — we think of them today,” the British leader said.
“It’s a moment for reflection, I would say, reflecting on how how things came to this,” he added.
Over the weekend, Arday cancelled events promoting his forthcoming memoir.
Publisher Simon & Schuster previously said that the book, Great And Unfortunate Things, would be published in the UK on 27 August.
In a statement on Saturday, the publisher said: “Simon & Schuster is deeply saddened by the news of Jason Arday’s tragic death, and we send our condolences to his family during this devastating time.”

title_zh: 剑桥前教授Jason Arday临终前感到无法继续生活
summary_zh: Jason Arday，前剑桥大学教授，因媒体的持续攻击而心理健康恶化。在他去世前的几个小时，他向朋友表示自己“无法继续下去”。Arday在童年时被诊断出患有自闭症、语言延迟和学习差异等障碍。在过去的十天里，媒体不断对他进行嘲笑、羞辱和抹黑，导致他的心理状态急剧恶化。最终，这些压力使他感到无法承受，选择结束自己的生命。
l1_lead: 媒体的持续攻击严重影响了前剑桥教授Jason Arday的心理健康，最终导致他选择结束自己的生命。
l2_summary:
前剑桥大学教授Jason Arday在临终前感到无法继续生活，原因在于他遭受了媒体的持续攻击，导致心理健康状况急剧恶化。Arday在童年时期被诊断出患有自闭症（autism）、语言延迟（language delay）和学习差异（learning differences）等障碍，这些问题使他的生活和学术生涯面临诸多挑战。在他去世前的几个小时，他向朋友表达了自己的绝望，表示“无法继续下去”。在过去的十天里，媒体对他的嘲笑、羞辱和抹黑不断升级，这种持续的心理压力最终使他感到无法承受，选择结束自己的生命。

这一悲剧突显了媒体对个体心理健康的影响，尤其是对于那些本就面临挑战的人群。Arday的经历提醒我们，社会对心理健康问题的关注和理解仍然不足，尤其是在面对自闭症和其他学习障碍时。媒体的负面报道不仅对个人造成伤害，也反映了社会对这些问题的偏见和误解。Arday的故事是一个警示，呼吁我们在讨论和报道心理健康问题时，需更加谨慎和同情，以免加重当事人的痛苦。

title: Appraisal of Gene Expression-Based Classifiers for Neuropsychiatric Disorders: A Meta-Regression.
body: A substantial body of research examines the potential of gene-expression-based biomarkers for diagnosing and selecting treatments for neuropsychiatric disorders, yet no clear consensus has been reached regarding the influence of controllable factors such as study design and model selection on the performance of gene-expression-based classifiers. To investigate study characteristics and methodologies that influence the accuracy of studies using transcriptomics to classify neuropsychiatric disorders, we conducted a literature review and meta-regression of relevant studies. We extracted several characteristics from each study, including the number of samples in a training dataset, approach for model validation, and classification model. Using univariate and multivariate mixed-effect meta-regression analyses, we estimated the association between these study characteristics and reported classification accuracies. Machine Learning (ML) models accounted for 55% of all models; Deep Learning (DL) models accounted for 20%, and variations of Logistic Regression models made up the remaining 25%. Support vector machine (SVM) was the most common model type (17%). The use of withheld test samples (56%) was the most frequent approach for validating the performance of classification models. We found significant associations between reported accuracies and study-rated bias risk, model type, class ratio, and validation approach. Overall, this review provides helpful insights into study characteristics that significantly influence classification accuracies and emphasizes the importance of prudent methodologies for training and evaluating classification models to mitigate biased accuracy estimates. In future research, these findings can direct study designs and support the development of clinically reliable, minimally invasive gene-expression biomarkers to improve diagnostic workflows and patient outcomes in neuropsychiatry.
journal: American journal of medical genetics. Part B, Neuropsychiatric genetics : the official publication of the International Society of Psychiatric Genetics
authors: Razavi A, Arensman B, Barnett EJ, Lee LA, Faraone SV, Glatt SJ, Hess JL.
title_zh: 基于基因表达的神经精神疾病分类器评估：元回归分析
summary_zh: 本文评估了基因表达生物标志物在神经精神疾病诊断和治疗选择中的潜力，探讨了研究设计和模型选择等可控因素对基因表达分类器性能的影响。通过文献综述和相关研究的元回归分析，提取了每项研究的多个特征，包括训练数据集样本数量、模型验证方法和分类模型类型。结果显示，机器学习（ML）模型占所有模型的55%，深度学习（DL）模型占20%，逻辑回归模型变体占25%。支持向量机（SVM）是最常见的模型类型（17%），而使用保留测试样本（56%）是验证分类模型性能的最常用方法。研究发现，报告的分类准确性与研究评估的偏倚风险、模型类型等因素之间存在显著关联。
l1_lead: 基因表达生物标志物在神经精神疾病的诊断和治疗中具有潜力，分类器性能受研究设计和模型选择等因素显著影响。
l2_summary:
本文评估了基因表达生物标志物在神经精神疾病诊断和治疗选择中的潜力，重点探讨了研究设计和模型选择等可控因素对基因表达分类器性能的影响。通过对相关文献的综述和元回归分析，研究提取了多项特征，包括训练数据集的样本数量、模型验证方法及分类模型类型等。结果显示，机器学习（ML）模型在所有模型中占比55%，深度学习（DL）模型占20%，而逻辑回归模型变体则占25%。在不同的模型类型中，支持向量机（SVM）是最常见的，使用比例为17%。此外，研究还发现，使用保留测试样本（56%）作为验证分类模型性能的最常用方法。

研究结果表明，报告的分类准确性与研究评估的偏倚风险、模型类型等因素之间存在显著关联。这一发现强调了在神经精神疾病的基因表达分类器研究中，研究设计和模型选择的重要性。通过对这些因素的深入分析，本文为未来的研究提供了重要的参考依据，指出了优化分类器性能的潜在方向。总的来说，基因表达生物标志物在神经精神疾病的诊断和治疗中展现出良好的应用前景，但其实际应用效果仍需在更为严谨的研究设计和模型选择下进一步验证。

title: Prevalence of attention deficit hyperactivity disorder/hyperkinetic disorder of pediatric and adult populations in clinical settings: a systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression.
body: Background Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD)/Hyperkinetic Disorder (HD) is linked to increased risks of morbidity, comorbidity and mortality, with higher prevalence in clinical populations. The differential prevalence of ADHD/HD across adult and pediatric clinical populations, influenced by factors such as time trends, sex, age, geographic regions, and comorbidities, has not been systematically assessed. Methods MEDLINE, CINAHL, Embase and PsycINFO databases were searched from inception to 1st August 2023 for eligible full-text papers published in English, and reviewing reference lists of identified studies and review papers. Studies reporting ADHD/HD prevalence in adult and pediatric clinical populations were included. Meta-regression evaluated the effects of geographic region, year of publication and sample size. Results From 30,740 citations, we reviewed 521 full-text articles, yielding 311 studies for inclusion (including 653,558 pediatric and 43,311 adult participants). Overall, worldwide pooled prevalence of ADHD/HD in clinical settings for pediatrics was 32.4% (95% CI 31-34%), and in adults 21.4% (95% CI 20-23%). Prevalence was higher in outpatient settings than inpatient settings. Prevalence based on rating scales was higher than studies using diagnostic interviews or clinical record review. Prevalence varied significantly across subspecialist settings for children and adults. No significant time trend was detected between 1981-2023. Pediatric prevalence appears influenced by geographic region but not year of publication or sample size. For adults, larger sample sizes were associated with lower prevalence estimates. Conclusions ADHD/HD prevalence in clinical populations is 8-9-fold higher than community estimates. With these patients at risk for many adverse outcomes, our findings underscore the critical importance of resource allocation for screening, diagnosing and treatment.
authors: Johnson S, Lim E, Jacoby P, Faraone SV, Su BM, Solmi M, Forrest B, Furfaro B, von Klier K, Downs J, Chen W.
title_zh: 临床人群中注意缺陷多动障碍的流行病学研究综述
summary_zh: 本研究系统评估了注意缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）/多动障碍（HD）在儿科和成人临床人群中的流行情况。通过检索MEDLINE、CINAHL、Embase和PsycINFO数据库，纳入了311项研究，涉及653,558名儿童和43,311名成人参与者。结果显示，全球儿科临床环境中ADHD/HD的合并流行率为32.4%（95% CI 31-34%），成人为21.4%（95% CI 20-23%）。门诊环境中的流行率高于住院环境，基于评定量表的流行率高于使用诊断访谈或临床记录审查的研究。此外，不同专业领域的流行率存在显著差异。这些发现强调了ADHD/HD在临床人群中的高发病率及其对公共卫生的影响。
l1_lead: 研究显示，注意缺陷多动障碍在全球儿科临床人群中的流行率为32.4%，成人为21.4%，强调了其对公共卫生的重大影响。
l2_summary: 本研究对注意缺陷多动障碍（ADHD，Attention Deficit Hyperactivity Disorder）/多动障碍（HD，Hyperactivity Disorder）在儿科和成人临床人群中的流行情况进行了系统评估。通过对MEDLINE、CINAHL、Embase和PsycINFO数据库的检索，研究纳入了311项相关研究，涉及653,558名儿童和43,311名成人参与者。结果显示，全球儿科临床环境中ADHD/HD的合并流行率为32.4%（95% CI 31-34%），而成人的流行率为21.4%（95% CI 20-23%）。研究还发现，门诊环境中的流行率显著高于住院环境，且基于评定量表的流行率普遍高于使用诊断访谈或临床记录审查的研究。此外，不同专业领域的流行率存在显著差异，这表明ADHD/HD在不同临床设置中的表现可能受到多种因素的影响。这些发现强调了ADHD/HD在临床人群中的高发病率，突显了其对公共卫生的深远影响，提示需要加强对该疾病的认识和干预措施，以改善患者的生活质量和社会功能。

title: Role of serotonin in psychiatric and somatic comorbidities of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic literature review.
body: Introduction Serotonin is a well-established modulator of various neuropsychological processes, as well as organ and endocrine functioning, and metabolism and homeostasis. Serotonin has been implicated in the neurobiology of attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). Herein, the evidence for a serotonergic link between psychiatric and somatic comorbidities associated with ADHD was evaluated. Methods A systematic literature review was conducted of the published literature to identify comorbidities proven to co-occur with ADHD and determine whether there was any serotonergic pathophysiology associated with these comorbidities. The average grade of serotonergic evidence was calculated and plotted alongside the volume of publications for each identified comorbidity. The date of the last search was 7 March 2024. Results One hundred eighty-two individual comorbidities commonly occurring in ADHD populations were identified; 135 (74.2 %) had evidence for serotonergic pathophysiology, including 91 psychiatric and 44 somatic conditions. The grade of evidence for a serotonergic role in the pathophysiology of a given comorbidity was generally medium to high or high. Conclusions Findings indicate that serotonin plays a key role, alongside dopamine and norepinephrine, in ADHD neurobiology. Serotonin involvement in physiological functioning suggests that dysregulation is likely to generate a broad spectrum of clinical manifestations, which may account for the unique presentation of neuropsychiatric behaviors and comorbidities found in patients with ADHD.
authors: Faraone SV, Ward CL, Boucher M, Elbekai R, Brunner E.
title_zh: 血清素在注意力缺陷多动障碍合并症中的作用
summary_zh: 本文系统评述了血清素在注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）相关的精神和躯体合并症中的作用。通过对已发表文献的系统性回顾，识别出182种常见的ADHD合并症，其中135种（74.2%）显示出与血清素相关的病理生理证据，包括91种精神疾病和44种躯体疾病。对每种合并症的血清素作用证据等级普遍为中等至高或高。研究结果表明，血清素在ADHD的神经生物学中与多巴胺和去甲肾上腺素共同发挥关键作用，其在生理功能中的参与暗示了其失调可能导致相关合并症的发生。
l1_lead: 血清素在注意力缺陷多动障碍的相关精神和躯体合并症中发挥关键作用，其失调可能导致多种合并症的发生。
l2_summary:
本文系统评述了血清素（serotonin）在注意力缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）相关的精神和躯体合并症中的作用。通过对已发表文献的系统性回顾，研究识别出182种常见的ADHD合并症，其中135种（74.2%）显示出与血清素相关的病理生理证据。这些合并症中包括91种精神疾病和44种躯体疾病，表明血清素在ADHD的合并症中扮演着重要角色。对每种合并症的血清素作用证据等级普遍为中等至高或高，进一步支持了血清素在ADHD相关病理中的重要性。

研究结果表明，血清素在ADHD的神经生物学中与多巴胺（dopamine）和去甲肾上腺素（norepinephrine）共同发挥关键作用。这种相互作用暗示了血清素在调节情绪、行为和生理功能中的重要性，且其失调可能导致相关合并症的发生。因此，血清素不仅是ADHD的一个重要生物标志物，也可能成为未来治疗策略的一个潜在靶点。综上所述，血清素在ADHD及其合并症中的作用值得进一步深入研究，以期为临床干预提供新的思路和方向。

title: Yes, ADHD diagnoses are rising, but that doesn’t mean it’s overdiagnosed
body: ADHD symptoms occur on a continuum and can fluctuate dramatically based on life circumstances such as transitions to middle school, stress levels and even sleep.
attribution_basis: The Conversation 作者页 /profiles/stephen-v-faraone-2397222（名+姓双命中）
title_zh: ADHD诊断上升，但并不意味着过度诊断
summary_zh: 注意缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）的症状呈现连续性，并且会根据生活环境的变化而显著波动，例如进入中学的过渡期、压力水平以及睡眠状况等因素。因此，尽管ADHD的诊断数量在上升，但这并不意味着该疾病被过度诊断。文章强调了ADHD症状的多样性和复杂性，指出在不同的生活阶段和情境下，症状可能会有所不同，从而影响诊断的准确性。
l1_lead: ADHD的诊断上升反映了症状的多样性和环境影响，并不意味着过度诊断。
l2_summary:
注意缺陷多动障碍（ADHD）的诊断数量近年来有所上升，但这并不意味着该疾病存在过度诊断的现象。ADHD的症状表现出明显的连续性，并且会受到多种生活环境因素的影响，例如进入中学的过渡期、个体的压力水平以及睡眠状况等。这些因素可能导致ADHD症状的显著波动，因此在不同的生活阶段和情境下，症状的表现和严重程度可能会有所不同。这种多样性和复杂性使得ADHD的诊断过程变得更加具有挑战性，影响了诊断的准确性。

文章强调，ADHD的症状并非固定不变，而是会随着个体的生活环境和心理状态的变化而变化。这种动态特性意味着，虽然诊断数量上升，但并不一定反映出对该疾病的误诊或过度诊断。相反，这可能是对ADHD认识加深的结果，促使更多的个体在面临相关症状时寻求专业帮助。因此，ADHD的诊断上升应被视为对该疾病理解和关注的提升，而非简单的过度诊断现象。

综上所述，ADHD的症状复杂多变，受多种因素影响，诊断数量的上升反映了对这一障碍的重视和理解，而非对其的过度诊断。这一观点为我们提供了更为全面的视角，以看待ADHD的诊断和管理。
l3_translation:
许多新闻媒体报道了注意缺陷/多动障碍（ADHD）在儿童和成人中的诊断数量增加或激增。同时，医疗保健提供者、教师和学校系统也报告了对ADHD评估请求的增加。

这些报告使一些专家和家长开始怀疑ADHD是否被过度诊断和过度治疗。

作为研究神经发育障碍（如ADHD）多年的研究人员，我们担心对广泛过度诊断的恐惧是错误的，可能是基于对这种疾病的根本误解。

关于ADHD过度诊断的讨论暗示着你要么有这种病，要么没有。

然而，当流行病学家询问普通人群中的ADHD症状时，有些人有一些症状，有些人有中等程度的症状，还有一些人有很多症状。但在被诊断为ADHD的人和未被诊断的人之间并没有明确的分界线，因为ADHD——就像血压一样——是一个光谱上的现象。

治疗轻度ADHD类似于治疗轻度高血压——这取决于具体情况。当医生考虑到一个人的日常生活细节以及症状对他们的影响时，护理可能会是有帮助的。

ADHD症状不仅因人而异，研究还表明，ADHD症状在个体内也可能发生变化。例如，当生活中的挑战增加时，症状可能会变得更加严重。

ADHD症状会根据许多因素波动，包括一个人是在学校还是在家、是否睡眠充足、是否承受很大压力，或者是否正在服用药物或其他物质。例如，轻度ADHD的人在度假并且休息良好时可能不会经历很多症状，但如果他们有一份要求很高的工作或学校日程，并且没有得到足够的睡眠，他们可能会出现影响生活的症状。这些人在某些情况下可能需要ADHD的治疗，但在其他情况下可能不需要治疗也能很好地应对。

这与高血压等疾病的情况相似，高血压可能会因一个人的饮食、压力水平和许多其他因素而在日常或每月之间变化。

ADHD症状通常在儿童早期开始，并且在儿童中期到晚期时通常最为严重。因此，平均诊断年龄在9到12岁之间。这个年龄段也是儿童从小学过渡到中学的时期，他们可能还会经历环境变化，这些变化会加重他们的症状。

从五年级开始，课程可能比早期年级更具挑战性。此外，过渡到中学通常意味着儿童从由一位教师在一个教室教授所有科目，转变为每节课都要换教室和不同的教师。这些变化可能会加剧之前控制良好的症状。

症状在一生中也可能时有波动。对于大多数人来说，症状在25岁之后会有所改善——但可能不会完全消失——这也是大脑通常完成发育的时期。

与ADHD常常共存的精神问题，如焦虑或抑郁，可能会加重已经存在的ADHD症状。这些状况也可能模仿ADHD症状，使得很难判断应该治疗哪种情况。高水平的压力导致睡眠质量下降，以及工作或学校的需求增加，也可能加重或引发类似ADHD的症状。

最后，某些物质的使用，如大麻或镇静剂，可能会加重甚至引发ADHD症状。除了使已经被诊断为ADHD的人症状加重外，这些因素还可能使轻度症状的人在短时间内发展为完全的ADHD。

反之亦然：一旦外部原因被消除，ADHD症状可以在不符合完全诊断标准的人身上减轻或逆转。

临床医生根据注意力不集中、过度活跃和冲动的症状来诊断ADHD。要在儿童中做出ADHD诊断，必须在这三类症状中至少有六种或更多症状存在。对于成年人，要求五种或更多症状，但这些症状必须在儿童时期开始。对于所有年龄段，症状必须在家庭、学校或工作等至少两个生活领域造成严重问题。

目前的估计显示，儿童中ADHD的严格流行率约为5%。在年轻成年人中，这一数字降至3%，而在60岁以上的人群中则低于1%。研究人员使用“严格流行率”一词来表示根据流行病学研究满足ADHD所有标准的人的百分比。这是一个重要的数字，因为它为临床医生和科学家提供了在特定人群中预计有多少人会患有ADHD的估计。

相比之下，“诊断流行率”是指根据医疗专业人员的实际评估被诊断为ADHD的人的百分比。在美国和加拿大，18岁以下儿童的诊断流行率在7.5%到11.1%之间。这些比例远高于5%的严格流行率。

一些研究人员声称，诊断流行率与严格流行率之间的差异意味着ADHD被过度诊断。

我们不同意这一观点。在临床实践中，诊断规则允许患者在大多数症状导致痛苦、损害或两者的情况下被诊断为ADHD，即使他们不符合完全标准。而且大量证据表明，诊断流行率的增加可以归因于对之前可能被遗漏的轻度病例的诊断。这些轻度诊断的有效性有充分的文献支持。

考虑一下那些有五种注意力不集中症状和五种过度活跃-冲动症状的儿童。这些儿童将不符合ADHD的严格诊断标准。

title: A Global Prospective Harmonization Framework for Suicidality, Anhedonia, and Obsessive-Compulsive Symptoms in Psychiatric Genetic Studies: A Cross-Continental Study Within the Ancestral Population Network.
body: This study aims to prospectively collect harmonized, quantitative, and dimensional psychiatric phenotypes (suicidality, anhedonia, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms) and information on discrimination, stigma, and unfair treatment in up to 27,500 individuals across diverse ancestries and clinical populations for genetic analysis within the NIMH Ancestral Population Network (APN). Five APN projects are participating in the current study (PUMAS-Paisa, PUMAS-NeuroGAP, KOMOGEN-D, LATINO, and SAX-II), spanning recruitment over 15 countries across the Americas, Africa, and Asia. Participants are being enrolled via the recruitment protocols specific to each participating project. The harmonized clinical battery includes the Columbia-Suicide Severity Scale, Snaith-Hamilton Pleasure Scale, and Florida Obsessive-Compulsive Inventory-II to assess suicidality, anhedonia, and obsessive-compulsive symptoms, respectively. Additionally, we use the Discrimination and Stigma Scale-Ultra Short to evaluate discrimination and stigma across cultures. This project is a pioneering effort to prospectively assess transdiagnostic phenotypes in large-scale, diverse ancestral and clinical populations (across different diagnoses) using a harmonized clinical battery, advancing genetic research in mental health in underrepresented populations.
journal: American journal of medical genetics. Part B, Neuropsychiatric genetics : the official publication of the International Society of Psychiatric Genetics
authors: Diaz-Zuluaga AM, Anderberg JL, Ramirez-Diaz AM, Marques AH, Rast CE, Bustamante D, Jonker D, Valencia-Echeverry J, Kyebuzibwa J, Muñoz JS, van der Walt K, Ramirez MC, Wootton O, Frederick RM, Stroud RE, Gur R, Rhee SJ, J
