title: Russia’s invasion of Ukraine is proof the EU needs to get better at stopping mass atrocities
body: The war’s one-year anniversary is eerily close to that of an EU report on the prevention of mass atrocities. Ten years later, its authors reflect on what the bloc could have done differently.
attribution_basis: The Conversation 作者页 /profiles/karen-e-smith-1415215（名+姓双命中）
title_zh: 俄罗斯入侵乌克兰证明欧盟需改善防止大规模暴行能力
summary_zh: 本文探讨了俄罗斯入侵乌克兰一周年之际，欧盟（EU）在防止大规模暴行方面的不足。十年前，欧盟发布了一份关于预防大规模暴行的报告，现今其作者反思该组织在应对当前危机时可以采取的不同措施。文章指出，欧盟在应对冲突和保护人权方面的能力亟待提升，以有效防止类似事件的发生。通过分析乌克兰战争的背景和影响，作者强调了加强国际合作和制定更有效政策的重要性，以确保未来能够更好地应对和预防大规模暴行。
l1_lead: 俄罗斯入侵乌克兰凸显了欧盟在防止大规模暴行方面的不足，亟需提升应对能力和国际合作，以有效应对未来危机。
l2_summary:
在俄罗斯入侵乌克兰一周年之际，欧盟（EU）在防止大规模暴行方面的能力显得尤为不足。十年前，欧盟发布了一份关于预防大规模暴行的报告，然而在当前危机中，作者反思该组织在应对冲突和保护人权方面的措施，认为亟需改进。文章指出，乌克兰战争的背景和影响凸显了欧盟在应对类似事件时的局限性，强调了加强国际合作和制定更有效政策的重要性。

作者认为，欧盟在防止大规模暴行方面的能力不足，导致其在面对俄罗斯的侵略时反应迟缓，未能有效保护乌克兰人民的基本人权。通过对乌克兰战争的深入分析，文章揭示了当前国际社会在应对暴行时的脆弱性，尤其是在协调各国行动和资源分配方面的缺陷。作者呼吁欧盟应当重新审视其防止大规模暴行的战略，强化危机应对机制，以便在未来能够更有效地应对类似的冲突。

此外，文章还强调了制定更为有效的政策的重要性，以确保在面对人道主义危机时，能够迅速采取行动，保护受害者的权益。作者指出，只有通过加强国际合作，才能在全球范围内建立起有效的防止大规模暴行的框架，从而避免历史悲剧的重演。

总之，俄罗斯入侵乌克兰的事件不仅是对该地区安全的挑战，也是对欧盟防止大规模暴行能力的深刻反思。文章呼吁欧盟在未来的政策制定中，必须更加注重人权保护和冲突预防，以确保能够有效应对和预防大规模暴行的发生。
l3_translation:
俄罗斯对乌克兰的入侵表明，识别大规模暴行风险并不是一个小众问题。许多人认为俄罗斯发动攻击是不理性的，因此低估了长期以来俄罗斯否认乌克兰国家地位和民族身份的言辞。如果政策制定者使用“大规模暴行视角”，他们就会看到侵略战争不仅是可能的，而且很可能伴随着大规模暴行，考虑到俄罗斯在车臣和叙利亚的历史记录。

对灭绝的恐惧解释了为什么乌克兰人感到他们在为生存而战，以及俄罗斯军队在布恰和其他地方犯下的暴行为何对任何和平协议的前景造成了重大打击。因此，关于大规模暴行的战略不仅是为了赋权欧盟拯救生命，还为了实现其在分裂世界中成为一个有原则的地缘政治行为者的宣言雄心，在冲突预防、管理和解决方面有效。

十年前，欧盟大规模暴行预防工作组发布了一份报告，评估了欧盟在预防和制止大规模暴行方面的优势和劣势。为了增强欧盟在这一领域的能力，我们建议它：

在战略政策文件和高层声明中明确承诺预防大规模暴行；

培养大规模暴行预防方面的专业知识，特别是国家/地区专业知识，并开展培训项目以提高专家的分析和预警能力；

加强其早期预警响应系统，以便更早地对大规模暴行风险采取行动；

通过外交手段，包括贸易和发展政策，以及与其他国际参与者的合作，减轻大规模暴行风险；

改善其快速反应正在进行的大规模暴行的能力。

欧盟在多大程度上按照我们的建议取得了进展，还有哪些改进的空间？

欧盟对大规模暴行预防的承诺分散在各种文件中。它没有像美国那样宣布将大规模暴行预防视为“核心国家安全利益和核心道德责任”。预防暴行犯罪被纳入了《2020-2024年欧盟人权与民主行动计划》等文件中，但没有纳入其他关键文件，如欧盟的《战略指南》，该文件评估了欧盟面临的安全挑战，并提出了加强欧盟安全和防御能力的具体建议。

欧盟理事会、欧盟的外交服务机构——欧洲对外行动署（EEAS）以及欧盟委员会都没有回应欧洲议会2013年对建立跨机构“保护责任共识”的呼吁。相反，欧盟2016年全球战略仅仅声明欧盟“将促进保护责任”（R2P），而没有指明欧盟如何积极保护人群免受种族灭绝、战争罪、反人类罪或种族清洗的侵害。

2016年，欧盟成为第一个任命“R2P联络点”的区域组织，该官员促进欧盟内部对暴行预防机制的协调，但我们无法从EEAS网站或组织图中辨别出当前欧盟联络点的身份，也没有发现与相关利益相关者的接触证据。尽管欧盟在联合国表达了对R2P的支持，但欧盟成员国对R2P日益政治化感到不安：例如，俄罗斯质疑在北约干预利比亚背景下R2P的合法性，但在其在格鲁吉亚和乌克兰的战争努力中提及R2P语言以为其合法化。

2018年底，EEAS发布了一份“暴行预防工具包”，帮助欧盟工作人员识别和应对暴行犯罪，列出了结构性风险指标、迫在眉睫的警告信号和减轻风险的具体措施。对冲突影响或脆弱国家风险的评估现在包括对仇恨言论的普遍性、社会不平等、大规模暴行的历史或未能承认过去虐待的分析。该工具包融入了自2014年以来建立的欧盟早期预警系统。

此外，欧盟的工具包在评估暴行风险时比联合国开发的工具包更进一步，采用了性别视角。然而，EEAS内部仍然存在一种根深蒂固的信念，认为关注人权、民主化和冲突预防就足以评估暴行风险并采取行动。

在全球人权制裁机制下，欧盟可以对负责侵犯人权的个人实施制裁，包括种族灭绝、反人类罪和战争罪，这在几内亚等案例中证明是成功的。欧盟的刑事司法合作机构EUROJUST运营着一个调查和起诉暴行犯罪的欧洲网络，并支持在乌克兰的联合调查小组。欧洲和平设施（EPF）围绕人权条件进行结构化，但在多大程度上考虑到大规模暴行风险仍不清楚。欧盟需要确保不允许在可能发生大规模暴行的背景下，政府获取军事装备。

欧盟正在发展一支5000人的快速部署能力（EU RDC）——这是对该集团当前1500名人员的欧盟战斗小组的重大升级。然而，目前的EU RDC规划场景中没有涉及预防或制止大规模暴行的重点。然而，如果适当训练并迅速部署，并被授权帮助保护平民生命，这些部队包可能在预防或减轻大规模暴行风险方面发挥关键作用，正如在塞拉利昂和北马其顿的预防性维和部署所示。

在过去十年中，欧盟采取了一些措施来增强其预防大规模暴行的能力，但还有很多工作要做。

title: Dans « Le Grand bain », un bataillon de mâles à la dérive ?
body: En plongeant ses héros dans une compétition de natation synchronisée, « Le grand bain » vient questionner la masculinité hégémonique et notre vision de la virilité.
attribution_basis: The Conversation 作者页 /profiles/thomas-bauer-1360183（名+姓双命中）
title_zh: 电影《大浴场》中的男性困境探讨
summary_zh: 电影《大浴场》以一名男性在花样游泳比赛中的表现为切入点，探讨了霸权男性气质（hégémonique masculinité）及其对男性身份的影响。影片通过展示男性角色在传统性别角色中的挣扎，质疑了社会对男性气质的刻板印象。通过对角色内心冲突和团体互动的描绘，影片揭示了男性在追求力量与脆弱之间的矛盾，挑战了观众对男性气质的固有认知。最终，影片引导观众反思现代社会中男性的身份认同及其对情感表达的压抑。
l1_lead: 电影《大浴场》通过男性角色的挣扎与内心冲突，探讨了霸权男性气质对身份认同的影响，挑战了对男性气质的刻板印象。
l2_summary:
电影《大浴场》通过一名男性在花样游泳比赛中的表现，深入探讨了霸权男性气质（hégémonique masculinité）及其对男性身份的影响。影片展现了男性角色在传统性别角色中的挣扎，质疑了社会对男性气质的刻板印象。通过对角色内心冲突和团体互动的细致描绘，影片揭示了男性在追求力量与脆弱之间的矛盾，挑战了观众对男性气质的固有认知。

在影片中，男性角色不仅面临外部社会对其身份的期待，还要应对自身内心的挣扎与不安。这种内心的冲突反映了现代社会中男性在情感表达上的压抑，尤其是在面对脆弱和敏感时的无所适从。影片通过对这些复杂情感的刻画，引导观众反思男性在当今社会中的身份认同问题，强调了情感表达的重要性。

影片的叙事结构和角色发展使得观众能够更深入地理解男性在传统性别角色框架下的困境。通过对角色之间互动的细致描写，影片不仅揭示了男性在力量与脆弱之间的矛盾，也让人们意识到这种矛盾是如何影响他们的自我认知和社会关系的。最终，影片促使观众重新审视男性气质的定义，鼓励对传统性别角色的反思与挑战，从而为男性在情感表达和身份认同上提供了新的视角。
l3_translation:
在奥林匹克运动会历史上，男性首次被允许参加艺术游泳比赛。自1984年洛杉矶奥运会引入这一体育项目以来，只有女性能够参赛。如果他们在2024年巴黎的参赛人数将受到限制（每支八人团队最多两名男性），这对于倡导包容性的人士来说，已经是一个巨大的胜利。

这一社会进步是简单的，还是男性长期斗争的结果，这一法规的变化让人想起了Gilles Lellouche的电影《大浴场》，该片于2018年上映。影片讲述了八名四十多岁和五十多岁的男性，他们在职业或情感生活中迷失，发起了一个挑战：赢得男子艺术游泳世界杯。

影片的评论在上映时获得了一致好评，毫无疑问与这一奥林匹克话题相关，质疑了性别研究中在法国较少涉及的一个角度，即与男性运动中的阳刚气质相关的刻板印象。

因此，可以看到《解放报》称其为一部“颂扬人类缺陷与脆弱”的喜剧，《费加罗报》认为这是部“将集体精神置于荣耀之上的社会电影”，而《巴黎人报》则表示这是“用无尽温柔诉说的人性真理”。导演（同时也是联合编剧）所进行的反思，确实可以用影片开头由一位旁白所提出的隐喻性公式来概括：一个圆能否进入一个方形？这暗示着，或许可以用一种不同于我们所被强加的方式来探讨运动与男性气质之间的关系。

Gilles Lellouche实际上为这些被时代所摧残的个体提供了一个慷慨的肖像，这一时代崇尚身体，而他们在“女孩的运动”中找到了救赎。这是对在普遍成功的压力下可能实现的自我成长的赞美，是团结战胜个人主义的胜利，是对抗普遍健美主义的柔软肚腩的展示，这部长片通过将团体治疗的主题转移到体育更衣室中，带来了新的气息。

如果法国公众被影片的故事所打动，那是因为该片反对一种本质主义的观点，即认为两性之间存在天生的差异。通过对父权制体系所推崇的阳刚气质的夸张，某些场景展现了一代人寻求意义的反英雄主义。这些人对经典的“霸权男性气质”进行了挑战，重新定义了21世纪法国社会中西方男性的形象。

该片灵感来源于真实事件，Gilles Lellouche的电影属于一系列对所谓“女性化”的男性这一代的无拘无束的虚构作品，这一代人不再被困于英雄式的阳刚气质模型中。

在撰写影片时，导演虽然想到了Peter Cattaneo关于工人阶级奇普恩代尔的电影（《全裸上阵》，1997年），但他主要受到2003年成立的瑞典男子艺术游泳俱乐部“斯德哥尔摩Simkonst Herr”的真实故事的启发，这是一个女性早已在政治和媒体生活中获得平等地位的国家。

这个俱乐部实际上还催生了一部纪录片和多部电影改编作品：《Allt flyter》由Måns Herngren执导（2008年）、《Men Who Swim》由Dylan Williams执导（2010年）、《Swimming with Men》由Olivier Parker执导（2018年）。这一主题在日本也找到了观众，Shinobu Yaguchi的喜剧《水男孩》和Song Haolin于2021年执导的同名中文改编作品。

选择艺术游泳，因其独特的女性特质（与其历史和两位美国电影芭蕾游泳女星Annette Kellermann和Esther Williams的成功相关），无疑是导演选择这一运动来阐述其观点的主要原因。

然而，我们也可以从第二层意义解读情节；游泳则可以被视为角色所面临困难及其想要摆脱困境的隐喻。这一理论从片名“《大浴场》”开始运作，在这个“浴场”中，每个人都必须跳入并学习在障碍中生存。

影片中的众多隐喻，编织出一种悲喜交加的叙事，使我们更好地理解导演超越刻板印象、学习自我接纳的愿望。实际上，水最初可以具有负面意义：它可以淹没、压倒甚至淹死。没有伸出的援手，缺乏足够的努力，往往很难独自将头从水面上抬起。

然而，Gaston Bachelard认为，滋养和包裹的水可以被视为一种积极的象征。这一元素的想象通常与母爱的联系在一起，因为它的形态与在我们体内寄居九个月的羊水相似，或与滋养我们的母乳相似。对Gilles Lellouche来说，游泳池恰恰是一个“非常母性的象征”，在影片中代表着“一个让人远离他人评判的茧”。因此，这些对生活感到失望的英雄们，投身于这个“母性浴场”，最终作为一个团结的群体重生，正如导演所说，感受到他们的心再次开始跳动。

通过这些在历史上被视为女性化的活动中找到救赎的男性的故事，《大浴场》引发观众对重新审视霸权男性气质的必要性的思考。它融入了当代的质疑，并且如同所说的那样，

title: Au cinéma, l’identité amérindienne trop souvent malmenée
body: A travers la figure du sportif, le film « Indian Horse » de Stephen Campanelli dénonce le racisme et les abus sexuels dont ont été victimes de nombreux amérindiens.
attribution_basis: The Conversation 作者页 /profiles/thomas-bauer-1360183（名+姓双命中）
title_zh: 电影《印第安马》揭示美洲原住民身份困境
summary_zh: 斯蒂芬·坎帕内利的电影《印第安马》通过运动员的形象，揭示了许多美洲原住民所遭受的种族主义和性虐待问题。影片不仅反映了历史上的不公正待遇，还强调了这些经历对原住民身份的影响。通过生动的叙述和角色塑造，电影引发观众对美洲原住民所面临的挑战的深刻思考，呼吁社会对这一群体的关注与理解。
l1_lead: 电影《印第安马》通过运动员的故事揭示了美洲原住民面临的种族主义和性虐待问题，强调历史不公对其身份的深远影响。
l2_summary:
斯蒂芬·坎帕内利执导的电影《印第安马》通过运动员的形象，深刻揭示了美洲原住民所面临的身份困境以及他们遭受的种族主义和性虐待问题。影片不仅反映了历史上对原住民的不公正待遇，还强调了这些经历对原住民身份认同的深远影响。通过生动的叙述和细腻的角色塑造，电影让观众得以深入理解美洲原住民在现代社会中所面临的挑战。

在影片中，运动员的奋斗与挣扎不仅是个人的故事，更是许多美洲原住民共同经历的缩影。电影通过展现他们在体育领域的努力与成就，揭示了更深层次的社会问题，呼吁观众关注这一群体的处境。影片中的角色不仅承载着个人的梦想与希望，同时也反映了整个族群在历史长河中所遭受的痛苦与压迫。

《印第安马》通过其叙事手法和情感表达，引发观众对美洲原住民身份的深刻思考。影片不仅仅是对个体经历的再现，更是对整个文化和历史的反思。通过对种族主义和性虐待问题的揭示，电影促使社会对美洲原住民的关注与理解，强调了在当今社会中，仍需为这一群体发声，推动更广泛的社会变革。

总之，斯蒂芬·坎帕内利的《印第安马》不仅是一部运动题材的电影，更是一部深刻的社会批判作品，揭示了美洲原住民在身份认同上的复杂性与困境，呼吁人们关注和理解这一历史悠久而又被忽视的群体。
l3_translation:
在Martin Scorsese的电影《月亮花的杀手》上映之际，这部关于1920年代奥萨吉美洲原住民鲜为人知的悲剧的史诗，我们重新发布这篇文章，提到其他近期的作品，并质疑美国产业中对美洲原住民的表现。

一位美洲原住民首领曾对白人说：“你们的文明将摧毁我们。但你们的魔法[电影]将使我们不朽。”这些话摘自加拿大纪录片Reel Injun，由Neil Diamond和Catherine Bainbridge制作（2009），如果将其置于背景中来看，显得极为深刻。因为在超过100年的历史中，电影产业制作了超过4000部关于美洲原住民的电影。正如Anne Garrait-Bourrier所解释的那样，这确实是“最常使用与印第安人形象相关的历史旧刻板印象的电影类型，将其作为‘故事’的中心，而这些故事与西部拓荒的现实毫无关系。”

好莱坞，尤其是从1930年代到1950年代的西部片，极度利用了印第安人的形象，并随着形势的变化（电影制作者的品味、制片人的意愿、观众的期待）而不断演变，从“血腥野蛮人”到“高贵的野蛮人”，再到“新世纪印第安人”。

然而，尽管运动在美洲原住民文化中是一个重要组成部分（正如许多传教士和人类学家的著作所证明的那样），但有一个方面却鲜为人知，甚至被轻视：运动员的形象。正是基于这一想法，电影制片人Stephen Campanelli在其2017年的电影《印第安马》中，借鉴了Richard Wagamese的小说，探讨了美洲原住民在传统与现代之间的身份问题，他们处于一种文化的夹缝中。

这位英雄面向西方生活，同时汲取其印第安遗产及相关的权利和义务，孜孜不倦地寻找自己的位置。影片讲述了一个年轻的奥吉布瓦男孩——Saul Indian Horse的悲剧故事，他在1961年被强行从家庭中带走，送入一所天主教寄宿学校，必须抹去自己的文化。

他暂时在冰球中找到了救赎，这项运动让他得以茁壮成长并加入一支职业球队。然而，他面临的潜在种族主义最终击垮了他。他放弃了，最终沉沦于酗酒和贫困之中。在经历了多年的流浪后，他在死神面前被及时救回，决定通过回到童年时光的地方来悔过。在那里，当他踏上圣杰罗姆寄宿学校的旧滑冰场时，他意识到——以闪回的形式——另一个一直困扰着他的恶疾：他曾遭受的性虐待。

寄宿学校在这里被描绘为一个痛苦的地方，是一种去美洲原住民化甚至文化灭绝的表现：影片中多次出现美洲原住民儿童遭受真实的心理和身体虐待的场景。必须指出，加拿大政府曾实施一项旨在根除土著语言和文化的政策，这为美洲原住民以及随后因同样原因受到影响的因纽特人所遭受的高酗酒、自杀和其他社会灾害的比例提供了背景。

基于Richard Wagamese的言论，导演Stephen Campanelli在片尾字幕中小心地提及了这些信息，并穿插了展示年轻美洲原住民在寄宿学校生活的档案影像：

“在1800年代末到1996年期间，超过150,000名土著儿童被送往寄宿学校。根据档案，至少有6,000名儿童在这些机构中去世。但估计还有成千上万的人。在2008年，加拿大政府最终道歉，并成立了一个真相与和解委员会，负责揭示真相。我们鼓励每个人敞开心扉，倾听因政府批准的激进同化政策而给几代土著儿童和家庭带来的痛苦与伤痛。”

阅读更多：
通过运动解放自己，打破性别刻板印象

通过回顾这些被牺牲的世代的历史，《印第安马》引发了一系列关于历史真相、当前社会条件以及这些在自己领土上变得陌生和边缘化的民族命运的讨论。这些痛苦证言的提及成为了重要的戏剧杠杆，通过这些杠杆，探讨了保留区的贫困、对酒精或毒品的依赖、社区间甚至家庭间的暴力等问题；这些都是导致一些儿童自杀的内心创伤。这部电影因此更新了一个电影类型，该类型长期以来倾向于在常常是非黑即白的情节中强加一个扭曲甚至羞辱的印第安人模型。

这一变化始于1970年代末，随着“亲印第安”电影的制作，旨在展示美洲原住民状况的更现实的视角，近年来则发展为一种超现实主义甚至失望的当代作品，如Chloé Zhao的《骑手》（2017）、Miranda De Pencier的《灰熊队》（2018），以及显然的《印第安马》。

如今的电影制片人，如Stephen Campanelli，给予美洲原住民自己发声的机会，没有修饰或虚假，没有可能使社区处于危险中的刻板印象。

Mispronunciations can occur. We are working with our partners to continually review and improve the results. Kitchener-based company Miovision, a global intelligence transportation system vendor, launched vehicle to everything (V2X) in Kitchener a few months ago. (Lauren Kuivenhoven/CBC) Social Sharing If you've ever found yourself second guessing whether you should speed up to make a green light, a new traffic light technology in Kitchener may help.
Kitchener-based company Miovision, a global intelligence transportation system vendor, launched vehicle to everything (V2X) in the city a few months ago.
It's a technology that connects traffic light information to cars, and lets drivers know when a light is going to be red or green by displaying a traffic light icon on the vehicle’s dashboard.
“Knowing what the signal is doing reduces your stress level dramatically … I know I don't need to rush because it's not going to do me any good,” said Thomas Bauer, the vice president of V2X at Miovision.
Thomas Bauer, the vice president of V2X at Miovision, explains how information from traffic lights is connected to cars. (Lauren Kuivenhoven/CBC) The traffic icon provides a countdown to green, the speed a driver must stay at to make a green light and a warning about when the light will turn red. Bauer says if a driver is going over the speed limit, the display will disappear.
The countdown to a green light will disappear four seconds before the light changes, “just to make sure that you are now looking out the window,” said Bauer.
He says the technology is meant as a driving assist for now, although it's a stepping stone toward autonomous driving.
Bauer says the technology offers both safety and environmental benefits. He says it’s especially valuable for heavy vehicles.
“They have a much longer braking distance. For them to know in advance if they're going to make a signal or not, this can be life or death.”
Bauer says knowing when to stop allows vehicles to save on fuel consumption, because they have more information on when to slow down for a traffic light.
Miovision started out by counting cars to help with transportation planning, and expanded to emergency vehicle pre-emption, which modifies the traffic signal to allow emergency vehicle or public transit through an intersection.
Miovision's V2X technology provides a countdown to a green light on a vehicle's dashboard. (Lauren Kuivenhoven/CBC) Now the company has launched V2X in Kitchener, which allows data from traffic lights to flow into vehicles over a cellular network.
“Kitchener is one of these cities in Canada where we have most of our equipment deployed. It's now available, I would say about 90 per cent of the intersections here,” said Bauer.
According to the Region of Waterloo, Miovision technology has been connected to traffic lights across the region since 2020.
In an emailed statement to CBC News, the region says the system uses cameras and other detection devices that are connected to the traffic signal controller.
Data is retrieved about cyclists, pedestrians and vehicles to "optimize the operation of the traffic signals,” said the statement, in part.
Kitchener-made tech connects cars to traffic light grid
September 1 | Duration closed caption 4:22 Miovision launched V2X in Kitchener a few months ago, a technology that connects traffic light information to cars. It lets drivers know when the light will turn red or green. Thomas Bauer, the vice president of V2X at Miovision, showed CBC K-W's Lauren Kuivenhoven how the technology works. With the new V2X technology, Bauer says instead of just collecting data about cars and intersections, the cars will be able to also receive data from the traffic lights.
"This is basically the reverse data flow. Instead of into the signal, it's from the signal back to the driver to influence the vehicle," said Bauer.
V2X currently covers more than 70,000 intersections across eight countries.
It’s available in VW Group cars, such as Audi, Bently and Porsche. Bauer says drivers can also download an app to connect the technology to their car, if they don't have a car brand from VW Group.

title: Royal Society president: GM crops feed much of the world today – why not tomorrow’s generations?
body: Science and technology has always helped us feed the world. GM has more to offer, if we let it.

title_zh: 皇家学会会长：转基因作物能持续养活未来世代
summary_zh: 皇家学会会长指出，科学与技术一直在帮助我们养活世界，转基因作物（GM crops）在这一过程中发挥了重要作用。当前，转基因作物已为全球许多人提供了食物，未来世代同样可以受益于此技术。文章强调，如果我们愿意接受转基因技术，它将为农业生产带来更多可能性，帮助解决全球粮食安全问题。通过科学的进步，转基因作物有潜力在应对气候变化和提高作物产量方面发挥更大作用。因此，支持转基因技术的应用将是确保未来粮食供应的重要策略。
l1_lead: 转基因作物在提高农业生产和应对气候变化方面具有重要潜力，是确保未来粮食供应的关键策略。
l2_summary:
皇家学会会长指出，科学与技术在养活全球人口方面发挥了重要作用，尤其是转基因作物（GM crops）在这一过程中扮演了关键角色。当前，转基因作物已经为全球数以亿计的人们提供了食物，未来世代同样可以从这一技术中受益。文章强调，若我们愿意接受转基因技术，它将为农业生产带来更多可能性，帮助解决全球粮食安全问题。随着全球人口的不断增长，粮食需求也在不断增加，转基因作物的应用能够有效提高作物的产量和抗逆性，从而在应对气候变化的挑战中发挥更大作用。

转基因作物的优势在于其能够通过基因工程技术，赋予作物更强的抗病虫害能力和更高的营养价值，这不仅能减少农药的使用，还能提高农作物的生产效率。科学的进步使得我们能够更好地利用这些技术，推动农业的可持续发展。支持转基因技术的应用被认为是确保未来粮食供应的重要策略之一，尤其是在面对气候变化带来的不确定性时，转基因作物能够为农业提供更强的适应能力。

总之，转基因作物不仅是当前解决粮食安全问题的有效手段，更是未来农业发展的重要方向。通过科学技术的不断进步，我们有理由相信，转基因作物将在未来的农业生产中发挥更为重要的作用，帮助我们养活未来世代。
l3_translation:
我的父母研究了印度的营养不良和缺乏营养，尤其是在儿童中，发现许多西方营养学家推荐的饮食实际上对贫困人群完全不适用。因此，他们制定了基于人们熟悉的本土食品的廉价健康饮食。然而，尽管他们进行了许多其他努力，印度有四分之一的人口和全球近九分之一的人口仍然没有足够的食物来过上健康活跃的生活。

世界银行估计，到2050年，我们需要生产大约50%的食品，以养活九十亿人口。在过去的50年中，农业生产力大幅提升——例如，美国的玉米产量翻了一番。但这伴随着化肥、农药和水的使用急剧增加，带来了自身的问题。也没有保证这种产量增长的速度能够持续下去。

正如新的农业技术和设备在中世纪促进了粮食生产，科学的作物育种、化肥和农药在20世纪的绿色革命中也发挥了作用，我们必须依赖最新技术进一步提升粮食生产。适当使用并进行适当监管的基因改造（GM）可能是解决方案的一部分。然而，基因改造仍然是一个高度争议的话题，不幸的是，基本事实常常被掩盖。

全球对基因改造的看法各不相同。美国几乎一半的作物是基因改造的，而在欧洲，由于广泛的反对，几乎没有基因改造作物种植。在加拿大，监管侧重于作物的特性，而在欧盟，重点则在于作物是如何被改造的。基因改造作物本质上并不会因其改造而对环境造成损害；基因改造仅仅是一种技术，我们应该关注和监管的是最终的产品，就像我们对待任何新产品一样。

在英国，有杰出的植物科学家从事基因改造研究，但苏格兰、威尔士和北爱尔兰政府已表示反对基因改造植物。在一个对科学家充满信任的国家，为什么会有如此强烈的反对？

大约15年前，当基因改造刚刚出现时，其主要支持者和许多初始产品来自大型跨国公司——尽管最初的许多研究是由公共资助的科学家进行的。可以理解的是，许多人认为基因改造是这些公司对作物施加垄断并最大化利润的一种手段。这种看法并没有因这些大公司的某些做法而得到改善，例如推出抗除草剂作物，导致除草剂的重度使用——这些除草剂往往是由同一家公司生产的。

辩论变得两极分化，任何理性评估证据的感觉都消失了。关于基因改造作物的负面健康影响和经济成本的说法也曾被提出——这些说法后来被证明是没有根据的。如今，英国一半的人对基因改造作物并不感到充分了解。

基因改造涉及将非常特定的基因引入植物。在许多方面，这比传统植物育种中选择的随机突变要更可控。我们认为自然的许多常见作物实际上与其野生祖先几乎没有相似之处，经过数千年的交叉育种，人类对其进行了选择性修改——从某种意义上说，这本身就是一种基因改造。

无论如何，我们在许多其他情况下接受基因改造：用于治疗糖尿病的胰岛素现在是由基因改造微生物生产的，几乎完全取代了动物胰岛素。例如，许多畅销药物是完全由基因改造生产的蛋白质，如抗体，现在占所有新药的三分之一（而且超过一半是销量最大的药物）。这些药物用于治疗多种疾病，从乳腺癌到关节炎和白血病。

基因改造已被用于创造抗虫害的植物，极大地减少甚至消除了对化学杀虫剂的需求，降低了农民和环境的成本。它还有潜力使作物更有营养，例如通过添加更健康的脂肪或更有营养的蛋白质。它被用于引入营养素，如β-胡萝卜素，人体可以从中合成维生素A——所谓的黄金大米——可以防止儿童夜盲症。而且基因改造有潜力创造抗旱作物——随着水资源的稀缺，这将变得越来越重要。

现在，全球超过10%的可耕地用于种植基因改造植物。美国国家科学院最近进行的一项广泛研究报告称，自18年前基因改造产品广泛商业化以来，没有证据表明消费任何批准的基因改造作物会产生不良影响。该报告还指出，没有确凿证据表明基因改造作物会导致环境问题。

基因改造是一种工具，我们如何使用它取决于我们。它当然不必是少数跨国公司的垄断。我们可以并且应该有足够的监管，以确保任何新作物品种（无论是基因改造的还是其他的）对我们自己和环境的安全，而我们有责任决定任何新植物中哪些特性是可以接受的。人们可能出于各种原因反对基因改造作物，最终消费者将决定他们想吃什么。但在贫困国家中，面临营养不良或饥饿的九分之一人口并没有享有这种选择。对他们来说，廉价、健康和营养丰富的食物的可获得性是生死攸关的问题。

除了其他农业实践的改进外，基因改造是解决全球粮食短缺的重要组成部分。然而，皇家学会的座右铭是“nullius in verba”；大致意思是“不要轻信他人的话”。我们需要进行充分知情的辩论。

title: Nobel Laureate Venki Ramakrishnan On Living Longer, Techie Arrogance, & Frontiers in Biology - India Currents
body:
原话：“When they were young, they wanted to be rich. And now that they are rich, they want to be young.” / “They see everything as a digital problem. Biology is analog, not digital.” / “When they freeze a mouse, unfreeze it, and it runs around, I’ll take notice.”
论点：科技行业的成功导致了对生物学的傲慢，认为生物问题可以用数字化思维解决。
论据：他指出，生物学是模拟的，而不是数字的，科技行业的人不愿意学习生物学。

They see everything as a digital problem. Biology is analog, not digital.

topic_zh: 对科技行业对生物学的误解的批评
claim_zh: 科技行业的成功导致了对生物学的傲慢，认为生物问题可以用数字化思维解决。

article_body:
Dr. Venki Ramakrishnan informed and entertained a packed audience at the South Asian Literature and Art (SALA) 2026 Festival at Menlo College, Atherton, CA on Sept 26 th , 2026, in a session entitled “The Science of Death,” moderated by science journalist Angela Saini.
In a discussion about his book Why We Die (William Morrow, 2024), Dr. Ramakrishnan switched from complex scientific topics, which he explained in simple, occasionally humorous terms, to engaging rants about Silicon Valley tech billionaires and their desire to prolong life.
Within a 7-mile radius of this place, people want to live longer, he said. Ramakrishnan observed that they can’t buy youth, but they can buy aging research, and that is distorting the field. He understands that scientists are abandoning UCSF, UCLA, and the Salk Institute and going to Altos Labs, because funding for research is a challenge.
Ramakrishnan amused the audience with lines like “When they were young, they wanted to be rich. And now that they are rich, they want to be young.” People in tech “see the brain as a computer,” he added. This is completely bonkers!”
He remarked that the arrogance that grew with successes in software shapes everything they see as a software problem. “They don’t bother to learn biology,” he said. “They see everything as a digital problem. Biology is analog, not digital.”
Later, he pointed out the inequities of living longer: rich people live approximately 15 years longer than poor people, he said.
Get stories like these directly in your inbox. Curated by us monthly to deliver the best of ours to you. Subscribe for free to our Arts & Culture newsletter - click here!
Skip the Scroll. Find nearby events you'll want spend time at and make new friends with our free weekly Events listing newsletter! Sign up here >>
Ramakrishnan also discussed aging research that has gained prominence in recent years, as governments grow “terrified” of a demographic cliff: fertility rates are plummeting, and they want to know whether people can be kept healthy for longer. Life expectancy has risen from about 40 to 60 to 80, explained Ramakrishnan, while rates for child mortality, infectious disease, heart disease and some cancers have declined. However, maximum lifespan is a separate question, he noted, giving examples of long life: the Galápagos tortoise, which may well have existed since the era of Darwin in the late 1800s, and Jeanne Calment, who lived to 122 with a daily cigar and glass of port after lunch and 2½ lb of chocolate a week.
“Evolution doesn’t care how long you live,” he commented; rather, it cares about reproductive success: A mouse reproduces early, makes lots of offspring and has a lifespan that’s short-lived.
Ramakrishnan said the idea of “biological age” is misleading because different organs age at different rates. He also called some anti-aging ideas “nutty,” including cryonics—the practice of freezing legally dead people in the hope that future technology might bring them back to life. He explained that cryobiology, such as freezing a mouse brain, only shows that a slice of tissue can be frozen. It does not prove that an entire person can be successfully preserved and revived.
Ramakrishnan remarked, “When they freeze a mouse, unfreeze it, and it runs around, I’ll take notice.
He argued that very little could be done with the vast amounts of data people collect from devices such as fitness rings or smart rings, commenting that it only contributed to more stress.
Dr. Ramakrishnan remarked that metformin and rapamycin may mimic some effects of calorie restriction as a way to slow aging; however, studies are still underway to determine whether they actually extend lifespan in humans.
He made a similar point about GLP-1 drugs, which he noted are “popular in California.” While they may have potential benefits for longevity, they affect many organs and can cause muscle loss, which also occurs with aging. He said proper clinical trials are needed to understand their long-term effects.
Dr. Ramakrishna’s book, Why We Die: The New Science of Aging and the Quest for Immortality, brings together biology, history, and ethics, making scientifically rigorous concepts accessible to a general audience. Kirkus Reviews called it “an illuminating account of the science of life extension with a more critical eye than most.“
In an exclusive interview with Raji Pillai for India Currents , Dr. Ramakrishnan discussed his journey, the next frontiers in science, and what lies ahead for him.
Raji Pillai lives in the San Francisco Bay Area and writes at www.rajiwrites.com. You can find her on Twitter at @rajiwrites2 More by Raji Pillai
title_zh: 诺贝尔奖得主拉马克里希南谈长寿与生物学的未来
summary_zh: 本文探讨了诺贝尔奖得主Venki Ramakrishnan对科技行业与生物学关系的看法。他指出，科技行业的成功导致了对生物学的傲慢，认为生物问题可以通过数字化思维来解决。他强调，生物学是模拟（analog）的，而非数字（digital）的，科技从业者往往不愿意深入学习生物学的复杂性。拉马克里希南用冷冻小鼠的例子说明，生物学的现象并不能简单地用数字化的方式来理解和处理。
l1_lead: 拉马克里希南强调生物学的复杂性，警示科技行业对其傲慢态度，认为生物问题不能仅通过数字化思维解决。
l2_summary:
诺贝尔奖得主Venki Ramakrishnan在探讨科技行业与生物学关系时，提出了对当前生物学研究方法的深刻反思。他指出，科技行业的迅速发展使得许多人对生物学产生了傲慢的态度，认为生物问题可以通过数字化思维来轻易解决。然而，拉马克里希南强调，生物学的本质是模拟（analog）的，而非数字（digital）的，这意味着生物现象的复杂性无法简单地用数字化的方式来理解和处理。他认为，科技从业者往往缺乏对生物学深层次复杂性的认识，导致他们在解决生物问题时可能会忽视重要的生物学原理。

为了说明这一观点，拉马克里希南以冷冻小鼠的研究为例，指出在生物学中，许多现象的发生和变化并不能仅仅通过数字模型来捕捉和解释。这种对生物学复杂性的忽视，可能会导致对生物现象的误解和错误的研究方向。他的论述提醒我们，生物学研究需要更深入的理解和探索，而不仅仅依赖于数字化工具和思维方式。

拉马克里希南的观点不仅反映了对生物学研究方法的批判，也为未来的生物学研究指明了方向。他呼吁科技从业者应当更加重视生物学的复杂性，深入学习相关知识，以便更有效地解决生物学领域中的实际问题。这一观点对于推动生物学与科技的结合，促进科学研究的全面发展具有重要意义。

article_body:
Scientists are pursuing the limits of longevity
By Venki Ramakrishnan edited by Clara Moskowitz
This article is part of a special package on “Impossible Questions”—scientific quandaries that may never get definitive answers. Read the rest of the collection here .
H umans may be the only creatures that are aware of their mortality. There is no evidence that other animals know their time on Earth is finite. The realization that we and everyone we know will someday die must be one of the more unsettling discoveries of childhood.
Ever since humans recognized we have a limited lifespan, that knowledge has shaped our cultures, religions and philosophies. Although we make plans, pursue careers and behave as though we will live indefinitely, the fear of death and the desire to transcend it remain.
As a species, we have made some major strides against mortality. In modern times, death from violence, disease and famine has become less common than it once was. At the same time, medical advances and a dramatic decline in fertility rates have produced aging societies. The proportion of people older than 65 is rising rapidly, while the working-age population that supports them shrinks. Understanding aging is therefore an urgent practical challenge. If we can delay its effects, older people may remain healthy, independent and productive for longer.
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing . By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
But alongside this public health imperative is an enduring dream. A growing number of tech billionaires are funding efforts not merely to slow aging but to defeat it altogether. Their goal is radical life extension and, ultimately, something approaching immortality. But is that even possible? These efforts have scientists chasing one of the biggest mysteries of life itself: Is there a biological reason that humans must die? And if not, could we one day live forever?
The diversity of lifespans in nature suggests that aging isn’t fixed. Despite being constructed from the same chemical building blocks, species can have dramatically different lengths of life. Mayflies may live only days, mice about two years, and bowhead whales and Greenland sharks for centuries. Galapagos tortoises live so long that one of them hobbling around today could have encountered Charles Darwin in 1835.
These differences are not random. Lifespan is closely related to metabolism. Smaller animals generally have higher metabolic rates and shorter lives; larger animals tend to metabolize energy more slowly and live longer.
Natural selection doesn’t care how long an organism lives. It favors traits that increase reproductive success. Every species makes trade-offs in how it allocates resources among growth, reproduction and maintenance. A mouse doesn’t improve its ability to produce more offspring by investing in longevity if starvation or predators are likely to kill it first. For a mouse, investing in rapid growth and reproduction is more advantageous. But larger animals, such as whales, mature slowly and reproduce later. Their bigger size also reduces the risk of predation, making long-term maintenance more worthwhile.
The same logic explains some notable exceptions. Birds and bats often live much longer than similarly sized terrestrial mammals because flight reduces the risk of predation and also allows them to forage over a wide area, cutting the chances of starvation. When surviving longer increases reproductive success, evolution favors slower aging.
Evolution can also reward genes that are beneficial early in life even when they become harmful later. For example, the same genes that promote rapid growth or prevent cancer during youth can contribute to aging later on. This evolutionary theory of aging is known as antagonistic pleiotropy. “Pleiotropy” simply means a gene can have more than one effect, and “antagonistic” means some of those effects can be harmful. The theory suggests that aging is not an adaptation in itself but an unintended consequence of evolutionary compromises. The upshot is that each species has a maximum natural lifespan.
Human life expectancy has roughly doubled over the past 150 years.
What about us? Human life expectancy has roughly doubled over the past 150 years because of improvements in public health, nutrition and medicine. Maximum lifespan is a different matter. Even centuries ago some individuals lived remarkably long lives. Michelangelo lived to be almost 90 years old. The longest documented human life is that of Jeanne Calment, who died at 122 in 1997. No one since then has lived past 120. Under current biological constraints, humans appear unlikely to live much longer than that. Moving much beyond it would require altering the biology of aging itself.
As people age, our muscle mass declines, reducing strength, mobility and balance. We suffer from fatigue and exhaustion and have difficulty carrying out everyday activities. Chronic diseases become more common, and resistance to infection weakens. Cognitive function declines as well. These symptoms are merely external manifestations of a gradual loss of cellular and tissue function, which themselves are a result of changes and damage to the molecules of life and their regulation by our genes.
Aging was once viewed as simple wear and tear, like a machine slowly breaking down, but modern biology has revealed a more complicated picture. Cells possess sophisticated systems for repairing damage, maintaining our repertoire of proteins, recycling components and regulating metabolism. Aging occurs not merely because damage accumulates but because these protective systems themselves become less effective over time.
The hallmarks of biological aging appear in multiple body systems. They include damage or changes to our DNA, deterioration of the quality and distribution of proteins, dysfunction of mitochondria, decline in our response to external nutrients, chronic inflammation, and reductions in stem cells. These systems are deeply interconnected—a disturbance in one often affects many others.
The encouraging news is that there is no physical or chemical law preventing us from modifying these processes. The challenge is that aging is extraordinarily complex.
Among the most powerful interventions discovered so far is caloric restriction. Animals given just enough calories to maintain adequate nutrition often remain healthier and live significantly longer. Caloric restriction reduces protein synthesis and stimulates autophagy, the cellular recycling process that removes damaged molecules and organelles. In species ranging from worms and flies to rodents and primates, caloric restriction produces animals that appear biologically younger than their age. The drawbacks, however, are considerable. Constant hunger, sensitivity to cold, impaired wound healing and reduced libido make strict caloric restriction difficult to sustain.
Scientists have searched for drugs that mimic some of the effects of caloric restriction without the side effects. One that appears promising is rapamycin, originally discovered in soil samples from Easter Island, also known as Rapa Nui by its native people. This compound affects a cellular pathway called TOR (or mTOR) that is involved in growth and metabolism. In mice, it extends lifespan and improves several measures of health. Yet rapamycin is also an immunosuppressant, raising concerns about infection and long-term safety. Current research focuses on whether lowering the dose or synthesizing chemical analogs of rapamycin can produce its beneficial effects without the problems.
Metformin, a widely used diabetes drug, has likewise attracted interest. It acts on a protein in mitochondria involved in respiration, which indirectly influences caloric-restriction pathways. Evidence for benefits in healthy individuals, though, is mixed. The recent GLP-1 drugs developed for diabetes and obesity also appear to have beneficial effects on multiple organs, including the brain. Yet they, too, have side effects, including muscle loss. For use as antiaging therapies, both metformin and GLP-1 drugs will require careful clinical trials.
Another major target of antiaging science is cellular senescence. Cells experiencing damage or stress sometimes enter a senescent state in which they stop dividing and begin secreting inflammatory molecules. Early in life this response is beneficial, aiding development, wound healing and cancer prevention. With age, however, senescent cells accumulate faster than the body can remove them.
The resulting inflammation contributes to tissue dysfunction throughout the body. In mice, eliminating senescent cells can improve many features of aging. This finding has sparked intense interest in so-called senolytic drugs designed to remove such cells selectively. Several candidates are now being tested against age-related diseases such as osteoarthritis and fibrosis. Apart from making sure the drugs are safe, the challenge is achieving the right balance: senescent cells serve a biological purpose, and eliminating them indiscriminately could lead to new problems.
Another, somewhat bizarre experiment has raised the prospect of a different antiaging strategy. In a process called parabiosis, researchers physically joined pairs of rats so they shared circulatory systems. Old rats paired with younger ones outlived those paired with animals their own age. Such findings went on to inspire a slew of companies offering transfusions of plasma from young donors. There is no convincing evidence that such procedures slow aging in humans. Nevertheless, the work has set off a major search for factors in blood that change with age and may eventually prove therapeutically useful.
Most of these approaches aim to slow down aging. A more radical goal is to reverse it.
This possibility emerged from a series of discoveries, spanning decades, involving the cells of the early embryo, which possess remarkable flexibility. These so-called pluripotent stem cells can generate any tissue in the body. In later stages, the stem cells become progressively more specialized, and each class generates specific types of tissue such as nervous system cells or blood.
In 1958 British biologist John Gurdon showed that the nucleus from a cell in a tadpole could be transplanted into an egg cell to create an entirely new frog. Later, in 1997, Dolly the sheep served as a demonstration that cloning was possible in mammals. The exact process for reverting adult cells back to an early embryonic stage, however, wasn’t clear.
A major breakthrough came in 2006, when Japanese biologist Shinya Yamanaka discovered that activating just four genes could convert adult cells into pluripotent stem cells. These Yamanaka factors effectively induce cells to return to an earlier embryonic stage by genetically reprogramming them. The discovery raised the possibility that if we can reset cellular age, perhaps we can reverse aging itself.
Applying the full reprogramming process to an adult organism would be dangerous because the resulting pluripotent cells could form tumors known as teratomas. Researchers therefore began exploring partial reprogramming, briefly activating the Yamanaka factors in ways that appear to rejuvenate cells while maintaining their specialized identities.
Results in mice have been striking. Treated animals often show improvements in tissue function and markers of biological age. In one experiment, scientists reportedly regenerated a damaged optic nerve by injecting Yamanaka factors via a viral carrier into the eye. Researchers are now conducting clinical trials to see whether the procedure can reverse degeneration in the retina or optic nerve.
Most antiaging approaches aim to slow down the process. A more radical goal is to reverse it.
Yet formidable obstacles remain. Curr
title_zh: 我们能否实现永生？
summary_zh: 本文探讨了延长人类寿命的可能性，指出尽管面临巨大复杂性，但细胞重编程（cellular reprogramming）是实现真正 rejuvenation 的最有希望的途径。衰老是一个涉及细胞、组织和器官之间无数相互作用的复杂过程，显著延长寿命需要同时掌握多个相关过程。尽管没有科学法则禁止这一想法，但实现这一目标仍然充满挑战。最终，这些研究发现是否能显著延长人类寿命仍然是一个悬而未决的问题。
l1_lead: 细胞重编程被认为是实现人类寿命显著延长的最有希望途径，但这一目标仍面临复杂挑战，尚无定论。
l2_summary:
本文探讨了延长人类寿命的可能性，特别关注细胞重编程（cellular reprogramming）作为实现真正年轻化（rejuvenation）的有希望途径。衰老是一个复杂的过程，涉及细胞、组织和器官之间的无数相互作用，因此显著延长寿命需要同时掌握多个相关的生物学过程。尽管目前没有科学法则明确禁止人类实现长生不老的想法，但在实际操作中，这一目标依然面临诸多挑战。

研究表明，细胞重编程可能通过恢复细胞的年轻状态，从而改善衰老相关的功能衰退。然而，衰老的机制极其复杂，涉及基因表达、细胞代谢、细胞间信号传递等多个层面，这使得科学家在寻找有效的干预手段时面临重重困难。尽管已有一些实验结果显示细胞重编程在动物模型中能够延长寿命，但将这些发现转化为人类应用仍需大量的研究和验证。

最终，尽管细胞重编程为延长人类寿命提供了新的视角和希望，但是否能够显著延长人类寿命仍然是一个悬而未决的问题。科学界对这一领域的探索仍在继续，未来的研究将有助于揭示衰老的本质及其潜在的干预策略。

title: Why We Die: a Nobel laureate in Chemistry tackles the killer question - European Scientist
body:
原话：“the hope of eternal life is therefore as illusory today as it has always been.” / “ageing is often a cause of disease, it is not itself a disease.”
论点：永生的希望是幻想，衰老本身不是疾病。
论据：消除所有导致死亡的衰老原因也无法使寿命延长超过15年。

quotes: the hope of eternal life is therefore as illusory today as it has always been.
ageing is often a cause of disease, it is not itself a disease.
topic_zh: 对生命延续与衰老的科学看法
claim_zh: 永生的希望是幻想，衰老本身不是疾病。
evidence_zh: 消除所有导致死亡的衰老原因也无法使寿命延长超过15年。
article_body:
In Why We Die, Nobel laureate Venki Ramakrishnan untangles the science of longevity from the fantasies of immortality. A welcome antidote to Silicon Valley's transhumanist intoxication.
If you are looking for a book that brings you up to speed on the science of longevity and the quest for immortality, get hold of Why We Die: The New Science of Ageing and the Quest for Immortality by Venki Ramakrishnan without delay. This Nobel Prize winner in Chemistry, recognised for his work on the structure and function of the ribosome, has also headed a research group at the MRC Laboratory of Molecular Biology in Cambridge and served as President of the Royal Society (the British Academy of Sciences) from 2015 to 2020. He is without doubt one of the scientists of his generation best qualified to address this subject.
In this short volume, published in 2024 by the British imprint Hodder Press, he offers non-specialists an accessible synthesis of what biology currently knows about this much-hyped topic — and dispatches the more nebulous theses doing the rounds.
A word of warning to fans of transhumanism: you are about to take a proper thrashing.
After an Egyptian curtain-raiser and a reminder of humanity's peculiarity — the only living being aware of the inevitability of death — the biologist cites the arguments of the philosopher Stephen Cave, who distinguishes four plans: plan A, living as long as possible; plan B, grounded in reincarnation; plan C, the immortality of the soul; and plan D, relying on what we leave behind, whether our work or our biological descendants.
For centuries, civilisations clung to these plans by developing various forms of religious belief (plans B and C). With the Enlightenment, the focus shifted to plans A and D. Modern science has allowed us to concentrate on plan A, and in particular on the wish to extend life expectancy as far as possible. Questions of stretching that expectancy — or even abolishing ageing itself — have come to the fore. The advances of modern biology make it possible not only to improve our health, but also to push back the limits of our lifespan.
In the past ten years, more than 300,000 scientific studies have been published, and more than 700 start-ups have poured tens of billions of dollars into trying to fight ageing… This has unleashed a wave of utterly wild hopes among Silicon Valley billionaires, the author observes, as he questions the soundness of the movement: 'Is it arrogant to think that we can cheat death using science and technology?'
A large question indeed — one that prompts the author to recall that one of his own main scientific discoveries is that ageing is bound up with the way the organism regulates the production and destruction of proteins. Ramakrishnan therefore sets out to take stock of the situation and of the avalanche of books on the subject, which are a decidedly mixed bag: ageing and mortality are multifactorial; while we may imagine prolonging life by aiming for better health, immortality itself remains entirely illusory. Here, then, is a synthesis of the points he develops to make his case.
One is grateful to the biologist for recalling what is specific about living organisms, drawing on notions that are almost finalist: first by daring the analogy between a cell and a city, then by reminding us that death shows itself as the disintegration of a whole… Those in the know will think of the French philosopher Raymond Ruyer's remark that none of our living cells has ever known anything but life, for millions of years, since they derive, by division or fusion, from other living cells, themselves derived from prevital molecules. While germline lineages persist, somatic cells are destroyed, Ramakrishnan reminds us.
The author quickly moves on to Darwin and evolution: natural selection eliminates lethal genes while still leaving individuals enough time to reproduce and contribute to the continuation of the species. Ageing is therefore indeed a Darwinian process. The Nobel laureate also proposes a taxonomy of the lifespans of living organisms according to two criteria — size and metabolism — and draws a general rule: the smaller and faster animals are, the more readily they tend to disappear, and vice versa. But of course there are many exceptions. As for humanity, the average has risen considerably with the progress of medical science; yet maximum age appears to be stagnating (the author cites Jeanne Calment's world record, still unsurpassed to this day), while according to Gompertz's law the risks of mortality grow exponentially with age.
Damage to cells (of which DNA is the command centre) is the process responsible for our death: the system charged with repairing our cells goes awry, and genomic instability increases. The author then turns to the options open to us for slowing this process, beginning with telomeres, whose shortening leads to the halt of cell division; one option might be to lengthen telomeres in order to rejuvenate tissues. He also considers what epigenetics, cloning and induced pluripotent stem cells have to offer — approaches that show living organisms can be 'partially reprogrammed'. Protein recycling matters too: ageing and the onset of neurodegenerative diseases are partly linked to its malfunction. In chapter 7 the author notes that certain experiments on yeast, worms, flies and mice have shown that eating less can lengthen life (setting aside, of course, malnutrition). A similar phenomenon is observed with rapamycin, a drug that allows one to eat less without chronic hunger. Ramakrishnan offers a tour of the solutions developed from discoveries by biologists: for example, creatures such as the worm C. elegans appear to possess a gene that extends life. From this have come solutions such as metformin, resveratrol…
While the first ten chapters are devoted essentially to advances in scientific knowledge and to technical problems, the last two open the debate more widely to 'science fiction' and to philosophy — notably chapter 11, entitled 'Crackpots or Prophets?', in which the biologist takes the transhumanists' — in his view — nebulous theses to task, starting with cryopreservation. The idea is not new, but it gained a new lease of life in the 1970s thanks to Robert Ettinger's foundation, which persuaded more than a hundred people to pay $28,000 to have their bodies preserved in containers filled with nitrogen. Several such firms exist today. Alcor is the best known. Ramakrishnan mentions the transhumanists who want only their brain preserved — and, since it is the seat of memory, to upload that memory onto a machine once the technology is mature. According to the biologist, there is little chance that this technology will ever work. By the time the body is cryogenised just after the individual's death, its cells may already have degraded irreparably… The technologies imagined for restoring the brain's configuration, such as connectomics, are in the author's view remarkably naïve, and above all they rest on no evidence or feedback from experience. Besides the fact that these transhumanists seem to ignore that the brain is intimately linked to the body, they tend to treat it as a machine only a little more advanced than a computer made of silicon.
The author then turns to Aubrey De Grey — an upper-class British eccentric — who is credited with the idea that the person who will live more than 1,000 years has already been born, because according to his 'escape velocity' thesis life expectancy rises steadily by several years with each passing year and describes a kind of exponential. To that end we must follow a seven-step plan (revitalise cells, remove senescent ones, prevent mitochondrial mutations…). De Grey's SENS programme has drawn heavy criticism from more than fifty experts in geriatrics, but he has thoroughly dismissed their replies.
Despite the many critical positions taken by experts in geriatrics, numerous commercial enterprises have plunged into the life-extension business. Yet Ramakrishnan recalls that eliminating all the causes of ageing linked to death could not increase life expectancy by more than about 15 years; the hope of eternal life is therefore as illusory today as it has always been. Whether antioxidants, telomere lengthening, hormonal supplements, calorie restriction, rejuvenation, or the cloning and replacement of damaged cells… all these techniques must be put into practice with the greatest caution. But such appeals from the scientific community have not stopped the anti-ageing business from prospering.
True, remarkable progress has been made; but one problem is that it is hard to say which treatments work without being able to run RCTs (randomised controlled trials)… given that this kind of trial seems impossible to conduct, and that it is difficult to claim one can improve what one cannot measure. Finally, while ageing is often a cause of disease, it is not itself a disease. Ramakrishnan then turns to a concept of the gerontologist James Fries: that we should all die young after a long life — which amounts to the compression of morbidity, resting on two assumptions: that we can delay the ageing process so as to postpone the onset of age-related disease, and that the length of life is fixed.
The final chapter is an almost philosophical framing of the question. First, even if we succeeded in slowing ageing, we would not prevent other causes of mortality (accidents, pandemics, violence…). Next, one can already see that the rise in average life expectancy has consequences for society that are not necessarily positive (pension problems, inequalities, costs for social security). A world of people who live longer would have to face the emergence of a form of conservatism, with a kind of inertia in power and in ideas, which would generate inequalities and conflicts between generations… wisdom, according to the author, therefore consists in settling for living as long as possible in good health, rather than aiming for eternal life.
One does not remain indifferent on reading this book, which describes what is specific to living organisms and denounces the paradigm that would confuse them with a machine that need only be fully reprogrammed, on the assumption that the whole in question equals the sum of its parts. The underlying philosophical question raised by the quest for immortality is that of the limits of what modifications of the living are possible. Yet in the AI revolution we are living through, fascinated by the all-powerfulness of LLMs and their apparent ability to pass the Turing test with flying colours, we tend to establish a continuum between the machine and the living organism. That fact is far from established. Experts working on these subjects ought, moreover, to ask themselves a prior question about the means of reaching that goal: is it easier to 'vitalise the inanimate' (imagine an android robot with all the qualities of a living individual and capable of replacing it — which is what I do in my novel Siliclone , for example) or to 'mechanise the living' (imagine reprogramming an individual as one programmes a machine)? The answer to that preliminary puts the sought-after objective and the path to it into perspective, and makes one aware of how far we still have to go.
Why We Die: The New Science of Ageing and the Quest for Immortality

article_body:

Nature has answered the same way for 3.5 billion years
Add Nautilus to Google 2 Comments There are all these people who say that death is natural, it’s just part of life, and I think that nothing can be further from the truth,” Peter Thiel told Business Insider in 2012. The venture capitalist has spent years backing efforts to slow or defeat aging, and his provocation captures the confidence of a wider Silicon Valley project: Given enough money and biological engineering, death may become just another technical problem to solve.
Nature, it seems, remains wholly uninspired by Silicon Valley capital. Scientific insight into 3.5 billion years of evolution suggests that death isn’t a glitch—it’s working as intended. That does not mean every organism carries a simple genetic suicide switch, or that every death is adaptive. It simply means that natural selection favors reproductive success over immortality. It also explains aging as the ultimate compromise for a body balancing the competing energetic requirements of development, reproduction, and repair.
“There is a cost to living, a cost to doing everything” Nick Lane, a biochemist at University College London, told Philip Ball in an interview with Nautilus . Lane examines life through the lens of energetics. He studies how much energy is required for life’s various processes, and how organisms go about acquiring and spending it.
“If we are living our lives at a very fast rate, we tend to, in effect, wear out sooner,” Lane said. Living is strenuous work. Growth, mating, pregnancy, parental care, and immune defense all consume energy and take a physical toll. Because maintenance and repair are themselves energetically costly, they must be traded off against these processes.
Across the animal kingdom, species have evolved different ways of allocating energy throughout their lives, mostly according to their size and exposure to external hazards. One consequence of this is that animals have vastly different natural lifespans.
Consider the mouse and the elephant. In the wild, a field mouse can live up to two years, whereas an elephant can live to 70. But mice are small and die easily, from predators or harsh weather. In such easy prey, natural selection is highly skewed toward early reproduction. An expensive body maintenance program for a distant (and highly unlikely) old age makes no sense. For an elephant, which matures slowly and faces fewer predators, evolution has selected for a durable body and a longer lifespan.
Overall, smaller species live fast lives, reproduce early, and die young. “There is a very strong relationship between metabolic rate, the rate at which we’re taking in oxygen and burning up food, and lifespan,” Lane said. This may help explain, at least partially, why caloric restriction can double or treble the lifespan of very simple organisms, like worms or fruit flies. Without calories, reproduction is unlikely and organisms enter a phase of “battening down the hatches and waiting out the bad times,” Lane said. But humans, of course, are far more complex. Our bodies are finely tuned to run at a metabolic rate held within narrow limits. Simply restricting calories in our diet would lead our bodies to burn up protein in muscle and other tissues.
In fact, humans are unusually long-lived for primates of our size. “Given our body mass, we live about twice as long [as we should for our size],” Venki Ramakrishnan, the Nobel Prize-winning structural biologist and author of Why We Die , told me. Improvements in nutrition, sanitation, and medicine have doubled the average human lifespan over the past 150 years, but our longevity has deeper roots. Michelangelo, Ramakrishnan noted, lived to nearly 90 in the 16th century, and some researchers believe human lifespans began lengthening as far back as 40,000 years ago. The drivers for the change remain unclear, Ramakrishnan said. A leading hypothesis links a sudden shift in human lifespan to the evolutionary perks of having grandparents in hunter-gatherer communities. Older adults helped raise children while parents were busy providing food. In times of crises, their accumulated knowledge of the environment gave their tribe a decisive edge in survival.
Given that modern humans have escaped many of the hazards that once made longevity a poor evolutionary investment, and that leaps in lifespan are possible, it makes sense to wonder if perhaps the billionaires have a case. Or, as Ramakrishnan put it, “The real question is, we have mechanisms for repairing damage, so why don’t we just keep repairing our body and live forever?”
The answer cuts to the heart of aging research.
Even in the absence of multiple stressors—we live comfortable lives indoors sheltered from environmental extremes and carry a significantly lower pathogen load than our ancestors—our bodies have evolved to keep the time. In 2022, Steve Horvath, a professor at the University of California, Los Angeles and a leading figure in anti-aging research, uncovered the existence of a molecular clock , a universal, internal mechanism that marks the age of mammalian cells and tissues. It reveals that aging is neither entirely random nor simply the accumulation of visible wear.
Throughout a cell’s life, patterns of chemical tags on DNA (called epigenetic markers) accumulate. Horvath developed a formula that reliably deciphers the pattern to predict the age of cells and tissues. This pattern is the “biological” age of the cell, which closely aligns with, but doesn’t always precisely map, chronological age. Its accuracy (for humans, it is exact to plus or minus 3.6 years) implies that aging is a carefully maintained biological process, rather than a haphazard set of events. We speed up the clock with things like smoking and excessive alcohol consumption.
Some scientists interpreted Horvath’s discovery—that all tissues count time—as indication that we are programmed to die, our cells marching inexorably toward death. But Horvath’s own interpretation swerves clear of such determinism and focuses instead on what the clock achieves in our early years.
We don’t think of babies as aging, but that is when the aging program is most active. Embryonic cells (which start off identical) need to differentiate quickly and in perfect synchrony into tissues, building organs and a body that continues to mature into adulthood. An internal metronome serves the essential function of orchestrating the elaborate process. But after adulthood, the program continues to run, and runs us all the way to the ground. “Evolution did not select a program that makes us die,” Horvath said. Instead, “Mother Nature never selected against it.”
As Ramakrishnan told me, “Death is an unintended consequence of aging.” And aging is an unintended consequence of development. Research shows that once development is complete (once we reach reproductive age), some of the genetic machinery that enabled it can keep running, or become reactivated as its regulation deteriorates, with increasingly harmful effects. In old mice, for example , the gene Hoxa9 , which is essential to a developing embryo, switched back on in muscle stem cells, activating obsolete developmental pathways that hindered muscle repair.
One of the hallmarks of aging is cellular senescence. It is a state in which damaged or stressed cells permanently stop dividing yet resist dying, accumulating in tissues over time. Though senescence initially protects against cancer by halting the growth of compromised cells, senescent cells secrete inflammatory molecules that harm surrounding tissue and drive many features of aging.
The runaway developmental programs of old age stem from the same evolutionary trade-off that links metabolism to lifespans. Selection prioritizes early biological performance (the period before reproduction happens) over late-life durability. A gene that promotes development or improves fertility and survival at 20 can be favored even if it raises the risk of degeneration at 70. A defect expressed only at 90 will encounter limited evolutionary pressure. Death is a compounding of the problem across a genome composed of genes all acting under the same selection. It is the final bill for evolution’s early favors.
All of this makes anti-aging innovations extremely challenging . Roughly 2,000 master control genes orchestrate early embryonic development, supported by another 5,000 to 10,000 organ-building genes. Re-tuning them for longevity without wreaking havoc is well beyond our current capabilities. “I don’t think it’s an impossibility, but it’s incredibly difficult,” Ramakrishnan told me.
The most immediate threat of getting this balance wrong is cancer. That’s because the signaling pathways that encourage cells to divide and repair tissues in early life are the exact same pathways that tumors hijack to proliferate unchecked. Override those aging pathways, and you remove the guards keeping malignancy at bay.
Researchers have already encountered this trade-off in one of the best-studied longevity pathways, which involves growth hormone (GH) and insulin-like growth factor 1 (IGF-1). Because IGF-1 promotes cell growth, muscle maintenance, and tissue repair, boosting its activity once seemed a plausible anti-aging strategy.
Read more: “ Physics Makes Aging Inevitable, Not Biology ”
But the same signals that encourage healthy cells to regenerate can also encourage precancerous cells to survive and multiply. Animal studies consistently show that reducing GH and IGF-1 signaling extends lifespan while lowering cancer incidence, whereas chronically elevated IGF-1 activity is associated with an increased risk of several cancers. The pathway that helps build and maintain the body in youth can become a liability when kept active into old age.
This compromise should not be entirely surprising. Adult stem cells possess an unusual capacity for long-term self-renewal, while cancer cells achieve essentially limitless proliferation by escaping the body’s normal controls. Efforts to make ordinary cells more regenerative inevitably edge them toward the biology of tumors. “An organism doesn’t want cells capable of indefinite reproduction,” Ramakrishnan said, “because that’s a cancer risk. You can think of senescence as evolution’s way of preventing cancer.”
The pattern is becoming uncannily familiar throughout aging biology: Molecules and pathways once cast as villains often turn out to have essential functions. For decades, scientists believed that aging was largely driven by the accumulation of damage from reactive oxygen molecules, or free radicals, produced by mitochondria. The theory was so influential that antioxidant supplements were widely promoted to slow aging. But decades of research have failed to support that idea.
Large clinical studies found little evidence that high-dose antioxidant supplements extend life or prevent age-related disease, and some have even linked them to worse outcomes. Rather than being merely destructive, Lane explained, free radicals act as vital cellular signals. “They are behaving a little bit like the smoke detector,” he said. When cells detect those signals, they activate genetic programs that repair damage, strengthen stress resistance, and help the cell survive. Blunting that signal indiscriminately is counterproductive. “The trouble with antioxidants is they’re in effect disabling the smoke detector,” Lane said.
A similar paradox occurs with anti-aging therapies that target the inflammatory response. Inflammation is essential
title_zh: 不朽是否可能？科学家的观点探讨
summary_zh: 本文探讨了延长人类寿命的可能性及其面临的挑战。科学家指出，尽管不朽并非绝对不可能，但实现这一目标极其困难，且可能带来癌症风险。生物体并不希望细胞具备无限繁殖的能力，因为这会增加癌症的风险。衰老（senescence）可以被视为进化防止癌症的一种方式。此外，约2000个主控基因协调早期胚胎发育，而调节这些基因以实现长寿的能力远超我们目前的技术水平。因此，延长寿命的尝试在现阶段仍然是一个充满幻想的领域，可能会分散我们对现实问题的关注。
l1_lead: 科学家认为，尽管不朽有可能，但实现这一目标极其困难，且可能增加癌症风险，因此延长寿命的尝试仍充满幻想。
l2_summary: 本文探讨了延长人类寿命的可能性及其面临的挑战，科学家们认为尽管不朽并非绝对不可能，但实现这一目标极其困难，且可能伴随癌症风险的增加。生物体并不希望细胞具备无限繁殖的能力，因为这会显著提高癌症的发生率。衰老（senescence）被视为一种进化机制，旨在防止癌症的发生，从而保护生物体的健康。研究表明，约有2000个主控基因在协调早期胚胎发育方面发挥着重要作用，而调节这些基因以实现长寿的能力远远超出了我们目前的技术水平。因此，尽管科学界对延长寿命的探索充满热情，但在现阶段，这一领域仍然充满幻想，且可能导致我们对现实问题的关注分散。总的来说，延长人类寿命的尝试在科学上面临诸多挑战，尤其是在平衡寿命延长与癌症风险之间的关系时，仍需进一步的研究和探索。

title: Venki Ramakrishnan, Nobel Prize in Chemistry: “At 108 years old, there is only a 50% chance of living one more - Diario AS
body:
原话：“there is no fundamental law of physics preventing humans from reaching 150 or even 200 years old” / “the human body accumulates layers of cellular damage that make that scenario extremely difficult to achieve.”
论点：人类寿命的上限并没有随着生活预期的提高而扩展，达到150或200岁非常困难。
论据：108岁的人生存一年只有50%的机会，且人类身体会积累细胞损伤。

quotes: there is no fundamental law of physics preventing humans from reaching 150 or even 200 years old
the human body accumulates layers of cellular damage that make that scenario extremely difficult to achieve.
topic_zh: 人类寿命的极限与衰老机制
claim_zh: 人类寿命的上限并没有随着生活预期的提高而扩展，达到150或200岁非常困难。
evidence_zh: 108岁的人生存一年只有50%的机会，且人类身体会积累细胞损伤。
article_body:
Ramakrishnan warns that radically extending human life would not depend solely on curing diseases.
The record for human longevity still stands at 122 years and 164 days —a benchmark untouched in nearly three decades since the death of Jeanne Calment. According to Venkatraman Ramakrishnan, recipient of the 2009 Nobel Prize in Chemistry, breaking past that boundary will take far more than medical breakthroughs designed to treat specific diseases. It would require intervening directly in the biological mechanics of aging itself.
Ramakrishnan argues that while life expectancy has surged over the last century and a half, the upper limit of the human lifespan has not expanded at the same pace. Standardized advancements in nutrition, sanitation, vaccines, antibiotics, and modern medicine have allowed far more people to reach old age, but the maximum cap on human life remains strikingly fixed.
The statistical probability of dying also climbs sharply as age progresses. According to data cited by the researcher in his book, Why We Die: The New Science of Aging and the Quest for Immortality , the odds of a 25-year-old dying within the next year stand at around 0.1%. That figure rises to approximately 1% by age 60 and hits 6% at 80. By age 100, annual mortality reaches roughly 16%, while a 108-year-old faces roughly a 50-50 chance of surviving another year.
While Ramakrishnan notes there is no fundamental law of physics preventing humans from reaching 150 or even 200 years old , the human body accumulates layers of cellular damage that make that scenario extremely difficult to achieve. Cells continuously work to repair DNA, eliminate damaged components, recycle proteins, and maintain mitochondria, but this internal maintenance machinery steadily loses efficiency over time.
Scientific research is currently exploring several avenues to slow this decline . One primary focus is caloric restriction, which in various organisms has shown a clear impact on metabolic pathways linked to aging and autophagy—the process by which cells clear out damaged components. However, those findings do not yet prove that drastically cutting food intake extends human life.
Researchers are also studying pharmaceuticals such as rapamycin, an immunosuppressant that targets the mTOR pathway involved in growth and metabolism and has successfully extended the lifespan of mice in lab trials. Applying rapamycin as an anti-aging therapy in humans presents major hurdles, however, largely due to its immunosuppressive side effects. Other drugs, including metformin and GLP-1 receptor agonists, are under similar scrutiny, though conclusive evidence that they can extend the lifespan of healthy individuals remains lacking.
Another frontier focuses on cellular reprogramming to partially reverse the aging process in cells. The use of Yamanaka factors has proven that a cell’s identity can be fundamentally reset, though complete cellular reprogramming inside a living organism carries severe risks, including tumor formation. As a result, scientists are developing methods for partial, controlled reprogramming aimed at restoring youthful cellular function without erasing the cell’s underlying identity.
Research continues to uncover additional biological barriers that could constrain extreme longevity. Among them is the accumulation of somatic mutations—genetic alterations that naturally occur within body cells over a person’s lifespan.
These findings suggest that even if scientists manage to master known mechanisms of aging, other biological hurdles will remain. For these reasons, the Nobel laureate in Chemistry maintains a cautious outlook on the prospect of radically extending the human lifespan.

title_zh: 拉马克里希南：人类寿命上限难以突破150岁
summary_zh: 诺贝尔化学奖得主Venki Ramakrishnan指出，尽管人类的平均寿命有所提高，但并没有科学依据表明人类寿命的上限会随之扩展。他提到，108岁的人仅有50%的机会再活一年，显示出高龄生存的困难。此外，人体在生命周期中会积累细胞损伤，这使得活到150岁或200岁变得极为困难。因此，尽管没有物理学的根本法则阻止人类长寿，但实际情况却使得这一目标难以实现。
l1_lead: 诺贝尔奖得主拉马克里希南指出，尽管人类平均寿命提高，但科学未能证明寿命上限会突破150岁，且高龄生存面临诸多挑战。
l2_summary: 诺贝尔化学奖得主Venki Ramakrishnan指出，尽管人类的平均寿命在不断提高，但并没有科学依据表明人类寿命的上限会随之扩展。他强调，现有的研究显示，108岁的人仅有50%的机会再活一年，这一数据反映出高龄生存的困难和挑战。随着年龄的增长，人体在生命周期中会积累细胞损伤，这种损伤是导致衰老和健康问题的重要因素。因此，尽管从物理学的角度来看，并没有根本法则阻止人类追求长寿，但现实中的生物学限制使得活到150岁或200岁变得极为困难。Ramakrishnan的观点提醒我们，虽然科学技术在不断进步，延长寿命的可能性依然存在，但突破人类寿命的极限仍然面临诸多挑战。

title: Science, Memory and Finding Your Voice: Three Conversations at The South Asian Literature and Art Festival 2026 - American Kahani
body:
原话：“Eat in moderation.” / “Get good, restful sleep.” / “Exercise in moderation.”
论点：他认为健康的生活方式应包括适度饮食、良好的睡眠和适度锻炼。
attribution_basis: Google News 全名命中 + LLM 同一人核验（American Kahani） + 论点方向独立复核
quotes: Eat in moderation.
Get good, restful sleep.
Exercise in moderation.
topic_zh: 关于健康和生活方式的建议
claim_zh: 他认为健康的生活方式应包括适度饮食、良好的睡眠和适度锻炼。
article_body:
The South Asian Literature and Art (SALA) Festival 2026 opened on September 26 at Menlo College in Atherton, California. This year’s theme is “The Global Gaze, The South Asian Soul.” Day 1 brought together voices from science, literature, mathematics, art, and journalism. I want to showcase the conversations with Nobel Prize laureate Dr. Venki Ramakrishnan, mathematician and novelist Manil Suri, and journalist, columnist, and author Shobhaa De.
Their disciplines are radically different, but their conversations touched on several universal questions: How do we make the most of a finite life? Where do our creative impulses come from? How does childhood shape the adult voice? And what does it mean to remain authentic?
Dr. Venki Ramakrishnan: The Science of Mortality
Dr. Venki Ramakrishnan brought a Nobel-level perspective with a gripping lecture on the science of death, aging, and mortality.
As a Nobel Prize laureate in Chemistry for his work on the structure and function of the ribosome, he made complex scientific ideas understandable to a lay audience. His core message challenged the current enthusiasm surrounding biohacking, cryopreservation of human brains, peptide treatments, and other promises of extending youth. Rather than approaching mortality through commercial hype, he encouraged the audience to understand aging through the lens of molecular biology. He discussed senescence and the shortening of telomeres, the prevalence of “skinny fat” among Indians and obesity in African Americans in the United States, and the relationship to stress.
An audience question sparked an important debate on lifespan and healthspan. The goal, he suggested, should not simply be to increase the number of years we live. What matters is the quality of those years. A longer life accompanied by frailty and cognitive decline is not necessarily the outcome we should be pursuing.
He also talked about the prime of life and creativity, particularly the period between ages 20 and 30. He cited examples such as Tolstoy writing War and Peace and the extraordinary creative output of Schubert, Mozart, Stravinsky, and other greats.
In a world increasingly obsessed with quantified health, Dr. Ramakrishnan offered surprisingly simple advice. Rather than relying on the data churned out of Oura rings and other devices, he recommended three timeless principles: Eat in moderation. Get good, restful sleep. Exercise in moderation. The idea that “what does not kill you makes you stronger” became part of a broader reflection on resilience and the value of living with purpose.
He used that the value of life lies in the pursuit of our ideals, even though our physical efforts eventually disintegrate.
Manil Suri: Mathematics, Memory and the Urgency to Write
Manil Suri is a rare talent who bridges higher mathematics and literature. A distinguished professor of mathematics at the University of Maryland, Baltimore County, he is also the acclaimed author of The Death of Vishnu, The Age of Shiva, and The City of Devi, as well as the memoir A Room in Bombay. He has also explored the relationship between mathematics and the universe in The Big Bang of Numbers.
Suri spoke about his desire to be surrounded by writers and poets. Although mathematics was his professional discipline, he felt that he was missing a dimension and wanted the companionship of the humanities.
He returned to a childhood habit of writing and initially committed himself to completing one story each year. “I got lucky and got published,” he said. When asked about the word “luck,” he explained that luck is about being in the right place at the right time.
Despite Suri’s modesty, his literary success is the product of discipline. Suri’s writing is deeply rooted in his childhood memories of Mumbai. He wrote regularly to his mother, who saved 2,711 of his letters. “One autumn, I just read all those old letters,” he recalled. “I picked up pieces of dialogue and memories hidden somewhere. They just need a trigger to come rushing back.”
Those letters became an unexpected archive of memory. His relationship with his mother and his experiences growing up in Mumbai formed the foundation of A Room in Bombay.
As someone who also grew up in Mumbai’s apartment complexes, I found his reflections deeply resonant. Many of us who grew up in those spaces will recognize the shared experiences, the proximity of neighbors, the sounds, the conversations, the sense of living among an interwoven tapestry of people’s lives.
When he signed my copy of The Death of Vishnu, it felt like a beautiful connection to those Mumbai roots.
We also discussed the urgency of writing what is clamoring to be written. That urgency is something many creative people understand: the feeling that an idea has become so insistent that it must find its way onto the page.
Suri has developed a disciplined routine around this impulse. He writes a sentence at night before going to bed and expands on it in the morning. He has also said that he can write before breakfast. Even one line. He has told his mind, “Today you will be writing.”
He believes the original thought is often the best. Language can be polished later.
His editing process is equally disciplined. For his memoir, he cut approximately 50 percent of a 140,000-word draft to find the story’s core.
He has become more adept at what he calls “self-editing.”
“When you are starting out, you tend to be self-indulgent,” he says. “You have to ask yourself: what is it that is driving the narrative forward?”
Shobhaa De: Finding the Courage to Use Your Voice
Shobhaa De stands as a pioneering Indian columnist, former supermodel, and bestselling novelist, often dubbed “India’s Jackie Collins.” In the 1970s and 1980s, she co-founded and edited legendary pop-culture magazines such as Stardust. Her novels, including Socialite Evenings and Starry Nights, boldly exposed both the glamorous and darker sides of urban India and Bollywood. Her voice has always been her defining characteristic: sharp, provocative, and unapologetic.
Her lecture on her latest book, The Sensual Self, moderated by Dr. Anjal Arondekari, had the audience in stitches. But beneath the humor, in an interview with me, was a thoughtful reflection on childhood, independence, family responsibility, gender, and the courage to take risks.
De’s fierce independence was forged early. As the youngest child in her family, she had greater freedom of self-expression than her older siblings. Yet she also felt intensely duty-bound to her parents. That tension between freedom and responsibility influenced the choices she made.
“Looking back, I could have taken many more chances,” she reflected. “But in a way, I was inhibited by not upsetting my parents more than they were already upset.
Her message to younger people is therefore deeply personal: “Just be reckless. Don’t play it safe. No safe bets.”
She remembered herself at five years old as “quite adorable,” but also “pampered, entitled, and a bit too obedient,” and wondered what she would tell that little girl today. “Enjoy being five years old, ” Shobhaa said, imagining herself.
Shobhaa said she did not have one “mentor” but the many people she admired in college and during her early journalism career, those who gave her “fantastic” breaks.
My friends and I grew up curled up on sofas reading her scandalous Stardust columns.
My father appreciated her tongue-in-cheek outspoken spirit. During our conversation, De revealed a magnetic aura that naturally encouraged people to open up to her.
We spoke about the troubling tendency among women in the West to muffle their own voices and shrink themselves to fit into a man’s world.
“There is no such thing as a man’s world. Don’t give it importance.”
She also spoke about ageism and the ways societies can impose limitations on women. Her message was that women must learn to rely on their own resources and continue to seek inspiration within themselves. Do not give up on yourself. Accept genuine care with grace but do not allow society to put you in a cage. On gender and identity, De made another characteristically memorable declaration. “I want to be reborn as a woman in the next seven lives.”
The three conversations explore different aspects of life: its limits, the power of memory, and the courage to express oneself. Together, they suggest that creativity grows from curiosity, personal history, and self-expression, connecting the global perspective with the South Asian experience.
With roots in Georgia and the Bay Area, and her heart still tethered to a childhood mango tree in Mumbai, India, Monita Soni approaches writing as a contemplative practice. A path to honor humanity. She has published hundreds of movie reviews, book critiques, poems, and essays, and contributed to combined literary works. Her two books are “My Light Reflections” and “Flow Through My Heart.” You can hear her commentaries on Sundial Writers Corner, WLRH 89.3 FM.

title_zh: 科学、记忆与寻找声音：2026年南亚文学与艺术节的三场对话
summary_zh: 本文探讨了在2026年南亚文学与艺术节上，科学家们对健康生活方式的看法。核心论点是健康的生活方式应包括适度饮食、良好的睡眠和适度锻炼。科学家们强调，适度饮食可以帮助维持身体健康，良好的睡眠有助于记忆和认知功能，而适度锻炼则能增强身体素质和心理健康。这些观点通过科学研究和数据支持，指出了健康生活方式对个人和社会的重要性，呼吁人们关注并实践这些健康建议。
l1_lead: 健康生活方式应包括适度饮食、良好睡眠和适度锻炼，这对个人和社会的健康至关重要。
l2_summary:
在2026年南亚文学与艺术节上，科学家们围绕健康生活方式展开了深入的对话，探讨了适度饮食、良好睡眠和适度锻炼对身体和心理健康的重要性。研究表明，适度饮食不仅有助于维持身体健康，还能有效降低慢性疾病的风险。科学家们强调，合理的营养摄入能够为身体提供必要的能量和营养素，从而促进整体健康。

此外，良好的睡眠被认为是提升记忆和认知功能的关键因素。研究显示，成年人每晚应保证7到9小时的睡眠，以便大脑在睡眠过程中进行信息整理和记忆巩固。缺乏睡眠不仅会影响学习能力，还可能导致情绪波动和心理健康问题。

适度锻炼同样被视为健康生活方式的重要组成部分。科学家指出，规律的身体活动能够增强心肺功能，提高身体素质，并有助于减轻压力和焦虑。根据相关数据，成年人每周应至少进行150分钟的中等强度锻炼，以达到最佳的健康效果。

通过这些科学研究和数据支持，科学家们呼吁公众关注健康生活方式的重要性，并积极实践这些建议，以促进个人和社会的整体健康。健康的生活方式不仅能改善个体的生活质量，还有助于降低医疗成本，提升社会的整体福祉。因此，适度饮食、良好睡眠和适度锻炼应成为每个人日常生活中不可或缺的部分。

title: From Kausar Munir To Venki Ramakrishnan, SALA Brings Diverse South Asian Voices Together - indica News
body:
原话：“There are no long-term clinical trials, and that’s what the science really needs.” / “Enjoy life; that’s going to make you live longer.” / “Look at data carefully before spending money on supplements.”
论点：流行的延长青春的饮食、冷冻技术等方法缺乏长期临床试验支持，科学需要更多数据。
