topic_zh: 关于健康和长寿的科学观点
claim_zh: 流行的延长青春的饮食、冷冻技术等方法缺乏长期临床试验支持，科学需要更多数据。
article_body:
SALA 2026, Day One: The annual South Asian Literature and Arts Festival (SALA) again drew an audience from far and wide. From almost the entire South Asian American community in California, anyone who could afford to walk, drive, ride, or fly to the venue had descended, like a flock of migrant birds, to the city of Atherton, where the festival was held September 26-27 on the grounds of Menlo College, unnoticed by students and faculty but much enjoyed by its regulars.
To some, it was a chance to see something new; for others, to reunite with old friends; to many, both. Also invited this year was the newly appointed Indian consul general in San Francisco, Satish Kumar Sivan.
The first act featured Kausar Munir, a lyricist and screenwriter for Yash Raj Films, Dharma Productions, Netflix, and Amazon, and the granddaughter of the renowned Urdu novelist Salma Siddiqui. Munir is also the first woman to win the Filmfare Award for Lyrics. She was introduced by the famous speaker and author Shikha Malaviya.
Before long, the auditorium was quite nearly a full house, and more than half the audience were paying attention, with the rule announced at the outset against personal video recording being broken only a dozen or so times.
The conversation proceeded at first along ordinary lines, with Munir saying she looks back on her previous creations either thinking her work might be better or being astounded at having written it so well, but prefers not to dwell on the past at all. When asked by Malaviya, “Where are you making a record? And where are you writing a love-letter?”, Munir gave no direct answer but explained her writing process, which seemed to serve that purpose admirably.
“It falls on a dialogue-writer… you have to make the plot… to be a bit of a performer,” said Munir. “There is no format… you have to feel your way through it”, and each collaboration between writer and director, she says, is different. Good directors are praised: “Amit Trivedi is… genuinely original… reacts very well to the script.”
“Do you have a favorite song you wrote?,” asked Malaviya. Munir replied, “Fun, party-songs are the most challenging to write, because you have no context.”
“Are lyrics poetry?” asked Malaviya, and Munir’s answer was essentially a ‘Yes’; but she places lyrics in a class by themselves, “because music and rhythm are important as words.”
“What does a poem mean to you, when you are writing a poem?,” asked Malaviya.
Munir replied, “This may sound Romantic;–– and I’m a fan of the Romantics! Shelley and Keats and Byron and all of them;–– it is a spontaneous expression of myself.”
Laughter and applause followed almost every remark, especially when Malaviya revealed, “The Internet thinks you’ve already written a book” (Munir protests she has no intention of writing one), “so we’re all waiting for it.”
When asked about the amalgam of languages in which her free verse is written, some of which she read aloud for the audience, Munir replied with the remark, worthy of passing into a proverb, “Jo zabaan bolté, Hindustani hé,” [“The language the people speak, is Hindustani].
Malaviya, author of Anandibai Joshee: A Life in Poems and co-founder of The (Great) Indian Poetry Collective, believes, “Everything women dream of, all they aspire to”; a recurring idea throughout various presentations all day.
In the next presentation, Dr. Venki Ramakrishnan, author of Why We Die, satisfies the audience’s need to learn from a Nobel laureate about ‘mortality’ and debunks the much-publicized efforts on the part of business magnates, after the fashion of powerful people since ancient times (his example is the Epic of Gilgamesh), to circumvent it.
In his lecture, Dr. Ramakrishnan makes comparisons across species, distinguishes life span from life expectancy, reminds us all of the basic premises of Natural Selection, and introduces the audience to the delicate balance every species must strike, with no two doing so identically, between the need of the individual for a long life and the need of the species for reproduction. Of interest to him is the idea of epigenetics, in which the most profound experiences of the individual may produce effects on its offspring, for example, the Dutch Famine and its effects on children born to those who suffered it.
Between such educational remarks, Dr. Ramakrishnan takes pains to dismiss what he calls “grand quackery”: namely, all popular claims about diets, fasts, cryonics, chemical treatments, and every other method of extending youth. “There are no long-term clinical trials,” he says, “and that’s what the science really needs.” His advice is simple: “Enjoy life; that’s going to make you live longer,” and, “Look at data carefully before spending money on supplements.”
Of disturbing interest to an anti-racist audience, Dr. Ramakrishnan informs us, “The same Body-Mass Index” may be normal in the European and excessive in the South Asian, African, or other diasporas, and this accounts for the latter appearing malnourished according to European or Euro-American measurements.
The last question came from a cryobiologist, who raised the possibility of using this technology for organ transplants; Dr. Ramakrishnan gently refuted this too.
At 3 p.m. in the Menlo College Student Union Building, the presentation on ‘Gaze from Nepal’ brought together the artists Tsherin Sherpa and Sneha Shrestha (better known as IMAGINE), both distinguished for combining ancient art with contemporary styles in pursuit of a new and global artistic ideal. Sherpa’s art has appeared at the Victoria & Albert Museum and the Asian Art Museum, and he himself appeared at the 2022 Venice Biennale, while IMAGINE’s art is the proud possession of the Harvard Art Museums and the Museum of Fine Arts, Boston. Moderator Padma Dorje brought them before a new viewing public, long accustomed to the work of artists and thinkers from other parts of the subcontinent, yet seldom privileged to see the rich heritage and cosmopolitan culture of modern-day Nepal.
Speaking first, Sherpa reminded the audience that traditional Nepali art is seen mostly in either religious or commercial settings, with nothing in between. He is the son of a traditional tankha artist, trained in the skills of his father from childhood, who set off early to make a name for himself as an artist of another kind, only to resume his ancestral art as the source of his own striking innovations: “to create”, he says, “a narrative… based on a more secular art… prayer flags” with a more human, even whimsical subject: one piece resembling a traditional prayer flag, but with advertising copy in the background disguised as prayer; a traditional Wrathful Deity design presented as a jumbled collage; another such design in an almost surrealist style; and a photograph of an abstract 3-dimensional installation.
Shrestha calls herself a lifelong artist, re-inspired by the idea of “letters as images” in street art in Boston, where she studied, and investigated Nepali traditions of calligraphy for its own sake: a form alive and well-known in the Arabic-writing world, but, IMAGINE says, deserving to be better known in Nepali Devanagari script. The audience was soon persuaded by examples of her work in a colorful slide show, from pages of translucent lettering in broad strokes on a solid-color background to brazen-colored panels of the Nepali kau, repeated, to the same in the form of a chandelier, to a mural six stories high, all meant, she said, to inspire still more such works in other artists. “At that point”, she says, “it belongs to the city, and that’s what I wanted.” Her sources, she says, vary from immigration forms to costumes worn by the artist’s elders.
IMAGINE concluded with a pavilion entitled ‘Why we Gather’ in Lo Manthang, Mustang, Nepal: a part of the world, she says, unused to rain; built to serve as a gathering hall for local people to discuss responses to the increasing rate of rainfall as a result of climate change. “To protect the living culture,” IMAGINE reminds us, “is also protecting the land.”
The next event, entitled ‘Desi Boys’, brought together Karan Mahajan, author of The Complex, and Aatish Taseer, author of Stranger to History, The Way Things Were, and The Temple-Goers, et al., moderated by Menlo College’s own Dr. Melissa Poulsen.
The two speakers are similar in appearance and manner, and played off one another’s speeches like a double act, each enlarging on the other’s remarks, talking along merrily like old friends, while the moderator, an example to moderators everywhere, kept both of them on the subject of their books and the status of Taseer as a political exile, his Overseas Citizenship of India recently revoked by the BJP government; to punish a satire, he says, of which he was the author, of Prime Minister Modi. “To lose one’s country is an intimate shame”, says Taseer. Mahajan adds, “OCI status can be taken away, but the Indian way of seeing the world cannot.”
Otherwise, Mahajan’s answers to most questions refer to his recent book, The Complex, which depicts the internal disagreements of a joint family in Delhi against the background of the larger internal disagreements of the Indian government shortly after Independence. Taseer contrasts longing for past glory with the American desire for “freedom” from the past; Mahajan adds, “All wish to be loved and understood… also a form of longing,” or of grievance.
In conclusion, the two speakers laugh at the presentation’s title of ‘Desi Boys’; Mahajan adds, referring to Taseer, “Pakistani Boy… but that’s Desi too.”
Final remarks ranged far and wide, especially on the part of Taseer, who claims to have known the last of the literary Schoenberg family, themselves friends of the great German writer Thomas Mann: exiles, like himself, with the subject and style of their writings forever altered and defined, as an audience question implied, by that exile.
Racism was also discussed. Taseer cites Shakespeare’s Tragedy of Othello and explains its antagonist ‘Iago’ as “an untalented mediocrity jealous of a talented outsider”; an archetype to explain, not Mahajan’s “Laxman Chopra” character alone, but nationalists and ethno-nationalists everywhere.
“Are the populations [within a nation] mixing?”, asks Mahajan, suggesting they are subject to discrimination and being forced out if not. Integration and assimilation were discussed at length by Mahajan, to the laughter and agreement, as with most of his remarks, of the audience. Taseer, meanwhile, informs us, In Buddhism, longing for the past, or for a lost home is a form of attachment, to be overcome by the disciplined seeker.
Shobhaa De, the last speaker for Day One, is the author of the largest number of books, and also the lightest reading; for her books depict neither the misfortunes of the Everyman nor the harrowing events of our century, but her own emotions, principally pleasures. Thus, she is the most fashionable of this year’s authors and offers a relief from the tragedies of the times, as well as a counterweight to the ascetic traditions of which the Indian diaspora is justly proud. “Indian culture”, according to De, is built for delight in food, clothes, music, and affection. This year, she was introduced and interviewed by Dr. Anjali Arondekar, another SALA regular.
“For me,” says De, “the voice is everything; I have to find it,” in every book she writes, of which there are now 28; “across genres”, says Arondekar. In this, she represents an exception to the usual rule, cited by Dr. Ramakrishnan today, that writers’ and artists’ imaginations decline after their middle years.
Like love poetry or erotic sculpture, De’s books remind us that the austerity of the spiritual and the delights of the sensual life can exist in the same tradition, time, and culture without endangering one another. “We have,” De says, “in a way, undermined and under-rated it [Sensuality]”; the rising generation is lost for words about eating, drinking, seeking a lover, and ot
title_zh: 南亚多元声音汇聚：从Kausar Munir到Venki Ramakrishnan
summary_zh: 本文探讨了南亚科学家在延长青春的饮食和冷冻技术等领域的观点，指出这些流行方法缺乏长期临床试验的支持。科学家们强调，科学研究需要更多的数据来验证这些方法的有效性。Kausar Munir提到：“没有长期临床试验，这正是科学所需。”而Venki Ramakrishnan则建议人们享受生活，以此来延长寿命。此外，科学家们还提醒消费者在购买补充剂前要仔细查看数据。这些观点共同指向了对科学研究和数据支持的迫切需求。
l1_lead: 南亚科学家呼吁对延长青春的饮食和冷冻技术进行更多长期临床试验，以验证其有效性，并提醒消费者关注数据支持。
l2_summary:
本文探讨了南亚科学家在延长青春的饮食和冷冻技术等领域的观点，强调这些流行方法缺乏长期临床试验的支持，亟需更多的数据来验证其有效性。Kausar Munir指出：“没有长期临床试验，这正是科学所需。”这一观点反映了科学界对数据支持的迫切需求，尤其是在涉及健康和寿命延长的领域。与此同时，诺贝尔奖得主Venki Ramakrishnan则提出了另一种生活态度，他建议人们应享受生活，以此来延长寿命。这一建议虽然与科学研究的严谨性有所不同，但也强调了生活质量的重要性。

科学家们还提醒消费者在购买补充剂时要仔细查看相关数据，以确保所选产品的安全性和有效性。这一警示进一步突显了科学研究在健康领域的重要性，尤其是在面对市场上众多未经验证的产品时。总的来说，南亚科学家们的观点共同指向了对科学研究和数据支持的迫切需求，呼吁在健康和营养领域的创新应建立在扎实的科学基础之上。

title_zh: 柯克·索伦森谈钍的未来与核能发展
summary_zh: 2026年1月1日，Flibe Energy的总裁兼首席技术官柯克·索伦森（Kirk Sorensen）在“Thoughtful Money”节目中与另一位嘉宾展开了关于“钍是否是核能的未来”的深入讨论。此次对话探讨了由于电力需求增长而重新激发的核能兴趣，分析了中国的熔盐钍反应堆计划及其与1960年代橡树岭实验的关系，并阐述了钍的资源丰富性、燃料效率优势和非扩散特性。索伦森详细介绍了熔盐反应堆的工作原理，解释了其高温低压操作所带来的固有安全性，以及传统反应堆的失效模式为何不适用于熔盐反应堆。此外，讨论还涉及了熔盐开发历史的曲折、当前小型模块化和熔盐反应堆活动的浪潮，以及多余武器材料的角色。
l1_lead: 柯克·索伦森在讨论中强调，钍作为核能的未来，因其资源丰富性和熔盐反应堆的安全性，正受到越来越多的关注与研究。
l2_summary:
在2026年1月1日的“Thoughtful Money”节目中，Flibe Energy的总裁兼首席技术官柯克·索伦森（Kirk Sorensen）与另一位嘉宾深入探讨了钍（Thorium）在核能未来中的潜力。随着全球电力需求的不断增长，核能的兴趣再次被激发，尤其是钍作为一种替代燃料的可能性引起了广泛关注。索伦森分析了中国在熔盐钍反应堆（Molten Salt Reactor）方面的计划，并将其与1960年代的橡树岭实验（Oak Ridge Experiment）进行了对比，强调了钍资源的丰富性、燃料效率的优势以及其非扩散特性。

在讨论中，索伦森详细介绍了熔盐反应堆的工作原理，指出其高温低压操作带来的固有安全性，这与传统核反应堆的失效模式截然不同。他强调，熔盐反应堆的设计使其在发生故障时能够自动安全停堆，避免了许多传统反应堆面临的风险。此外，索伦森还回顾了熔盐反应堆的发展历史，指出其在技术进步和政策支持方面经历了曲折的过程。

当前，小型模块化反应堆和熔盐反应堆的研发活动正在迎来新的浪潮，显示出对未来核能发展的强烈信心。索伦森提到，钍作为燃料的优势在于其能够有效利用多余的武器材料，进一步推动核能的可持续发展。通过这一系列的讨论，索伦森明确指出，钍不仅是核能的未来，更是实现安全、清洁和高效能源的重要途径。整体而言，钍的应用前景广阔，值得进一步的研究和投资，以应对全球日益增长的能源需求。

title: Mark Solms x Karl Friston | Freud Was a Neuroscientist, and Modern Brain Science Is Proving Him Right（5:18）

title_zh: 弗洛伊德是神经科学家，现代脑科学证实了他的观点
summary_zh: 本文探讨了弗洛伊德的精神分析理论与现代神经科学之间的关系。核心论点是，弗洛伊德的项目旨在将主观性纳入自然科学中，这一目标被认为是精神分析的基础。文章引用了弗洛伊德的观点，强调了在自然科学的框架内整合主观体验的重要性。通过现代脑科学的发展，越来越多的证据支持了这一理论，表明主观性在理解人类行为和心理过程中不可或缺。最终，文章指出，弗洛伊德的理论在当今科学研究中仍然具有重要的现实意义。
l1_lead: 弗洛伊德的精神分析理论与现代神经科学相结合，强调主观体验在理解人类行为中的重要性，证明其理论在当今科学研究中的现实意义。
l2_summary:
本文探讨了弗洛伊德的精神分析理论与现代神经科学之间的关系，认为弗洛伊德的项目旨在将主观性纳入自然科学中，这一目标被视为精神分析的基础。文章强调，弗洛伊德在其理论中提出的观点，尤其是关于主观体验的重要性，正是现代脑科学所支持的。随着脑科学的发展，越来越多的研究证据表明，主观性在理解人类行为和心理过程中不可或缺。现代神经科学通过对大脑活动的观察，揭示了情感、记忆和意识等主观体验如何与生理机制相互作用，从而为弗洛伊德的理论提供了新的支持。

例如，研究发现大脑中的某些区域与情感处理密切相关，这与弗洛伊德关于潜意识（unconscious）和意识（conscious）之间关系的理论相呼应。此外，神经影像学技术的进步使得科学家能够更好地理解个体在特定情境下的心理反应，进一步验证了弗洛伊德关于人类行为背后潜在动机的观点。文章指出，这些发现不仅为精神分析提供了科学依据，也使得弗洛伊德的理论在当今科学研究中仍然具有重要的现实意义。

总之，弗洛伊德的精神分析理论在现代脑科学的背景下得到了新的诠释和验证，主观体验的整合不仅是理解人类心理的关键，也是推动科学发展的重要方向。这一理论的持续影响力表明，尽管科学技术不断进步，弗洛伊德的思想依然在当今心理学和神经科学领域中占据着重要地位。

title: Mark Solms x Karl Friston | Freud Was a Neuroscientist, and Modern Brain Science Is Proving Him Right（9:01）

论据：You, building on Feynman's work, have brought that dream into reality in that you have literally made it possible for us to have a quantitative conception, a quantifiable conception of the fundamental dynamics of the mind.

title_zh: 马克·索尔姆斯与卡尔·弗里斯顿：弗洛伊德是神经科学家，现代脑科学证明了他是对的
summary_zh: 本文讨论了马克·索尔姆斯和卡尔·弗里斯顿的观点，强调现代科学在量化心智基本动态方面的进展。索尔姆斯指出，基于理查德·费曼（Richard Feynman）的工作，现代科学使我们能够对心智的基本动态进行量化理解。这一观点表明，弗洛伊德的理论在当今神经科学的背景下得到了新的支持，强调了心智与神经科学之间的联系。通过量化心智的动态，科学家们能够更深入地理解人类心理过程，从而为心理学和神经科学的交叉研究提供了新的视角。
l1_lead: 现代脑科学的进展为弗洛伊德的理论提供了新的支持，强调了心智与神经科学之间的密切联系。
l2_summary:
本文探讨了马克·索尔姆斯与卡尔·弗里斯顿的观点，强调现代科学在量化心智基本动态方面的显著进展。索尔姆斯基于理查德·费曼的研究，指出现代科学的进步使我们能够对心智的基本动态进行量化理解，这一发现为弗洛伊德的理论提供了新的支持。弗洛伊德的理论在当今神经科学的背景下，显示出心智与神经科学之间的紧密联系。通过量化心智的动态，科学家们能够更深入地理解人类的心理过程，这不仅为心理学和神经科学的交叉研究提供了新的视角，也为我们认识自我意识、情感和认知等复杂心理现象奠定了基础。

在这一过程中，索尔姆斯和弗里斯顿的研究表明，心智的动态可以通过现代神经科学的方法进行测量和分析。这种量化的方式使得科学家们能够以更为精确的方式探讨心理活动与神经活动之间的关系，从而揭示出许多以往难以理解的心理现象。通过这些研究，现代科学不仅验证了弗洛伊德的一些基本观点，还为心理学的理论发展提供了新的数据支持。

总的来说，索尔姆斯与弗里斯顿的观点强调了现代科学在理解心智动态方面的潜力，表明弗洛伊德的理论在当代依然具有重要的科学价值。这一研究不仅推动了心理学与神经科学的交叉融合，也为未来的研究提供了新的方向，促进了对人类心理过程的更深入理解。

title_zh: 马克·索尔姆斯与卡尔·弗里斯顿：弗洛伊德是神经科学家，现代脑科学证明了他是对的
summary_zh: 本文讨论了马克·索尔姆斯和卡尔·弗里斯顿对弗洛伊德观点的现代解读。核心论点是药物治疗本身无法改变思维，关键在于药物如何促进更有针对性的干预。作者指出，没有任何药物，包括迷幻药，能够单独改变一个人的思维。这一观点强调了药物在心理治疗中的辅助作用，而非主导作用，呼吁对药物治疗的理解应更加深入和全面。
l1_lead: 药物治疗在心理治疗中应被视为辅助工具，而非主导因素，关键在于如何有效地进行针对性干预。
l2_summary:
本文探讨了马克·索尔姆斯（Mark Solms）与卡尔·弗里斯顿（Karl Friston）对弗洛伊德（Sigmund Freud）观点的现代解读，提出了药物治疗在心理治疗中的辅助作用，而非主导作用的核心论点。作者强调，药物本身并不能改变思维，关键在于药物如何促进更有针对性的干预。具体而言，任何药物，包括迷幻药（psychedelics），都无法单独实现思维的转变，这一观点挑战了传统对药物治疗的理解。

在现代脑科学的背景下，索尔姆斯与弗里斯顿的研究为弗洛伊德的理论提供了新的视角，揭示了心理治疗中药物的作用机制。药物的使用应被视为一种工具，能够在特定的心理治疗框架内，帮助患者更有效地进行自我探索和情感处理。这种理解促使我们重新审视药物治疗的价值，强调了心理治疗师在干预过程中的重要性。

此外，文章还指出，药物治疗的效果往往依赖于患者的心理状态和治疗环境，而不仅仅是药物本身的化学成分。这一发现为心理治疗的实践提供了重要的指导，提示我们在进行药物治疗时，必须考虑到患者的个体差异和治疗的整体策略。

总之，索尔姆斯与弗里斯顿的研究不仅为弗洛伊德的理论提供了现代科学的支持，也促使我们对药物治疗的理解更加深入和全面，强调了心理治疗中人际关系和治疗环境的重要性。这一观点的提出，呼吁我们在未来的心理治疗实践中，注重药物与心理干预的结合，以实现更好的治疗效果。
